From our experience, the cotton bud/rubbing alcohol method works best. As with the DualSense, it's also worth updating your Xbox Wireless Controller's firmware. To do this, press the Xbox button on your pad, then navigate to Profile and system > Settings > Device and connections > Accessories. Choose your controller, and if there's a new firmware update available, install it. You should also download the Xbox Accessories app from the Xbox Store. This free software has calibration tools that allow you to adjust/test the dead zones of your controller's sticks. What causes stick drift? The most common cause of stick drift is simple wear and tear. The more you use your controller, the greater the chance stick drift will occur. If you've used your gamepad for hundreds of hours, there's a decent chance you'll eventually encounter this annoying defect. Controllers use devices called potentiometers to track the position of their analogue sticks, and these can wear down after heavy usage. Accidental damage and moisture build-up can also cause stick drift. Sweat and liquid can impact the internals of your gamepad, in turn affecting its sticks. Even new controllers can be hit with stick drift. You might end up being unlucky by picking up a pad that has calibration problems straight out of the box due to manufacturing issues. Should you find your sticks are playing up and your controller is still under warranty, definitely try to get it repaired or replaced by Microsoft or Sony.

item.title: Your car's dash cam might be illegal in some states — Here's how to check
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.33
Your car's dash cam might be illegal in some states — Here's how to check Before you head out on a road trip, make sure you won't be accidentally breaking the law. Dash cams are useful for so many reasons. They capture footage while you're driving, and some record motion even when you're parked. The footage one captures can prove invaluable in the event of an accident or break-in, since the recording can be presented as objective evidence. Yes, dash cam footage that is captured in a public place and can be authenticated should hold up in court. That's the main purpose of using one. But along with safety and record-keeping, you could use one to monitor driving habits of teens, capture other incidents that happen to occur in its view, like road rage or fraud (think someone jumping in front of the car to claim injury), or even just record the beautiful scenery on your drive. While dash cams are legal in every state, there are specific rules about how you can use them, where to position them and even their size that vary from state to state. Even if you know the laws in your own state, if you're driving out of state for a road trip, it's important to know the laws in others. The last thing you want is to be driving with a piece of equipment positioned or being used illegally in your car. The rules around dash cam use The rules when using dash cams in different states vary considerably. The simplest and most logical rule is about positioning, requiring that a dash cam not obstruct the view of the driver. This rule explicitly applies in Alaska, Arizona, California, Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Missouri, Nevada, North Carolina, Utah, and Vermont. However, it's a logical rule you should follow everywhere. Some of those states have specific rules about camera placement beyond ensuring it doesn't obstruct your view. In California, for example, a dash cam has to be mounted in a seven-inch square on the lower corner of the windshield, away from the driver, a five-inch square in the corner nearest to the driver, or in a five-inch square in the upper-center. Meanwhile, in Illinois, a dash cam must be in the bottom corner of the windshield on the passenger side. In some states, like Alabama, Delaware and Louisiana, the dash cam can't even be mounted on the windshield at all, while states like Pennsylvania and Minnesota forbid having anything mounted on a windshield, period. In these cases, it has to be mounted on the dashboard. So, it's important to check positioning rules in your state. There are also size requirements, with most states requiring that a dash cam be smaller than five inches. Some states, like Hawaii, permit dash cams as large as 7 inches, while in Indiana, it can be no more than 4 square inches. When it comes to use, in 13 states, you can't record conversations in a vehicle unless every passenger in it consents. The 13 states where this two-party or all-party consent rule applies are California, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington. Other states have rules about recording that you should pay attention to as well. In states like New York and many others, recording video from a dash cam is fine. But audio conversations are not permitted without at least one party's consent. This might not matter much for family road trips, but it's something to consider if you're traveling with colleagues, carpooling with others outside your family, or are a ride-share driver. How to prepare for a drive Because there's no single federal rule about dash cam usage and installation, you need to be cognizant of the specific rules in any state you're traveling to or even through to ensure that you adhere to the local laws. Your best bet is to use the most stringent rules of any of the 50 states and adhere to them to avoid problems while you travel. California is a good benchmark to use, since it's widely considered to have among the strictest laws for dash cam placement and usage. The good news is that dash cams in general are legal to have and use in every state, so simply having one won't get you nabbed for doing anything wrong. Just make sure it doesn't obstruct your view in any way, and get a small 4- or 5-inch model. Consider mounting it on the dashboard instead of the windshield if you're worried about positioning. Another option is to mount it behind the rearview mirror. If placed here, the dash cam doesn't obstruct any part of your view that isn't already obstructed by the mirror itself. Use a mount that's easy to remove and reposition if you must do so to adhere to local law as you're passing through. Before you head out on the road, if you're crossing state lines, map your route. Then check the state Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) website to see the specific rules in each state when it comes to dash cams. From there, position the dash cam according to the strictest rule for visibility. If necessary, disable audio recording if you're entering a state with two-party consent rules, or make clear to everyone in the vehicle that audio is being recorded. With proper preparation, you can get the most out of your dash cam and make sure you're following the law, no matter where you are.

item.title: Can a MacBook run multiple external monitors? It depends
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.28
Can a MacBook run multiple external monitors? It depends Most current models support at least two. A MacBook isn't just a portable computer. It can also double as the heart of a desktop workstation. To do that, you need at least one external display. But how many can you connect? Well, it isn't just a matter of how many ports your laptop has. It's more about the chip inside. Apple's current lineup ranges from the budget MacBook Neo, which only supports one external display, to the M5 Max MacBook Pro, which can drive up to four. Resolution and refresh rate variables prevent this from being a cut-and-dried answer, but the basics are simple enough to understand. Apple's current MacBook lineup Here's how Apple's current lineup breaks down: - MacBook Neo – one external display - MacBook Air (M5) – two external displays - MacBook Pro (M5) – two external displays - MacBook Pro (M5 Pro) – three external displays - MacBook Pro (M5 Max) – four external displays These figures aren't affected by whether you're using the built-in screen. In other words, clamshell mode (closing the MacBook's lid) doesn't raise the limit. Resolution and refresh rate Resolutions and refresh rates are where we start to get into the weeds. For example, the M5 MacBook Air supports up to two 6K displays at 60Hz or two 4K displays at 144Hz. If you only want one display? Then you can do 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 240Hz. Here's a more detailed list with resolutions and refresh rates: - MacBook Neo - Maximum: one 4K display at 60Hz - MacBook Air (M5) - One display: Up to 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 240Hz - Two displays: Up to two 6K at 60Hz or two 4K at 144Hz - MacBook Pro (M5) - One display: Up to 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 240Hz - Two displays: Up to two 6K at 60Hz or two 4K at 144Hz - MacBook Pro (M5 Pro) - One display: Up to 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 240Hz - Two displays: One up to 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 240Hz - Plus a second up to 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 200Hz - Three displays: Up to three 6K at 60Hz or three 4K at 144Hz - MacBook Pro (M5 Max) - Can drive many combinations, including: - Up to two 8K displays at 60Hz - Up to four 6K displays at 60Hz - Up to four 4K displays at 144Hz - Can drive many combinations, including: These are Apple's official maximum configurations, but your results could vary depending on several factors: your specific cables or adapters, the resolution and refresh rate of your monitors and which dock you use. MacBook Neo: the most limited model The MacBook Neo is a surprisingly capable laptop for its mere 8GB of RAM, but external display support is one area where it shows its limits. Although it has two USB-C ports, only one can drive a single external display. One important thing to note: the port closest to the back of the laptop is the high-speed (USB 3) connection, and only it can support video output. The most you'll get out of it is one external display at 4K resolution and a 60Hz refresh rate. The further-forward (USB 2) port can't carry a display signal and is limited to less demanding accessories or charging. The Neo also doesn't support Thunderbolt, so Thunderbolt-only displays and accessories aren't part of the deal. That limited support may be all you need for a simple home office setup. But if you want to hook up multiple monitors or something like, say, a 5K ultra-wide, the MacBook Neo isn't the machine for you. Thunderbolt docks and USB hubs If you're setting up a full-on workstation for your MacBook Pro or Air, a quality Thunderbolt dock can be like a miracle worker. It lets you connect multiple accessories through a single cable: external displays, storage drives, keyboards, mice, Ethernet and more. It can even power your MacBook on top of that. But even the best Thunderbolt dock (looking at you, CalDigit) doesn't automatically increase your MacBook's display output. It can make your setup easier and, in some cases, route multiple monitors through one port. But pushing past Apple's display limits isn't in the cards. (And remember, the Neo doesn't even work with Thunderbolt.) Basic USB hubs are even more limited. Although some include HDMI or DisplayPort output, they still can't raise your MacBook's official display limit. DisplayLink: A cheat code for some setups If you want to go over Apple's official limits, DisplayLink is the most popular workaround. However, there are caveats. It does this through a combination of hardware and software. First, you need a DisplayLink-compatible dock or adapter. Then, install the DisplayLink Manager app on your Mac and grant it Screen Recording permission. The software compresses the display image and sends it over USB to the DisplayLink chip inside the accessory. It then converts that signal into video for your monitor. This can allow you to connect displays beyond Apple's official limits. For basic office work, it might be all you need. But keep in mind that it isn't a great solution for more visually demanding tasks like gaming. In addition, some copy-protected video streams (including Netflix, Disney+, and YouTube TV) may not play at all while a DisplayLink screen is connected, though local video and basic YouTube should be fine. If your dock supports both native video output and DisplayLink, use the former when possible. You'll get better refresh rates and responsiveness, without any content-blocking concerns. Save DisplayLink for those "break glass" scenarios where you need more displays than your Mac officially supports. Older models: Where to start We narrowed the scope here to Apple's current MacBook lineup, but what about older models? Well, some of the rules are different there. For example, on some past MacBooks, the number of supported displays increases when your laptop is closed. For those details, it isn't hard to find Apple's official specs. You can identify your MacBook model by clicking the Apple menu (upper-left corner of the screen) and clicking About This Mac. Then look up your model's external display specs on Apple's support website.

item.title: The One Mistake That Could Ruin The Total Solar Eclipse In Spain
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.63
Topline With only days remaining until the total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, thousands of eclipse chasers are making their final travel plans for northern Spain. However, many could still miss the spectacle if they overlook one crucial detail — this eclipse happens just before sunset. Although the path of totality crosses northern Spain, the totally eclipsed sun will sit exceptionally low above the northwestern horizon, where mountains, trees and buildings could easily block the brief moments of totality. Fortunately, there is still time to check viewing locations using a growing range of eclipse-planning websites, apps and horizon tools. Key Facts On Wednesday, Aug. 12, the moon’s dark central shadow will sweep across eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain, creating a total solar eclipse along a path approximately 190 miles (305 kilometers) wide. Unlike Spain, the eclipse occurs high in the sky from Greenland and Iceland. Within that narrow corridor, observers will experience up to 2 minutes 18 seconds of totality, when daylight briefly fades and the sun’s faint outer atmosphere, the corona, becomes visible to the naked eye. Outside the path, only a partial eclipse will be visible. Across Spain, the height of the eclipsed sun varies dramatically. In Galicia, totality will occur with the sun about 11 degrees above the northwestern horizon. By the time totality reaches Spain’s east coast, the sun will be only about 4 degrees above the horizon, and just 2 degrees from the Balearic Islands, leaving little margin for error. The Balearic Islands — Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera — present perhaps the greatest challenge. There, totality occurs only minutes before sunset, making an unobstructed northwest horizon absolutely essential. For example, Mallorca’s capital, Palma, Spain’s eighth-largest city, will have its view of the eclipsed sun entirely blocked by mountains to the west. For those who choose their location carefully, Spain’s eclipse promises one of the most dramatic astronomical spectacles seen from mainland Europe since 1999. A totally eclipsed Sun hanging just above the horizon minutes before sunset could produce extraordinary views and unforgettable photographs. Why Sunset Makes This Eclipse Different For many visitors, everything will depend on choosing a viewing site with an unobstructed view of the northwest horizon. It’s common for people to completely misunderstand the geometry of a total solar eclipse and fail to get into the path of totality. However, Spain’s rare sunset eclipse creates a unique challenge because even observers inside the path of totality could lose sight of the eclipsed sun if it drops behind local terrain before totality begins. Choosing a location within the path is critical, but finding a clear view low toward the northwest is just as important. High ground, open farmland, reservoir shorelines and exposed coastal viewpoints are all likely to offer better prospects than wooded valleys or cities. Last-Minute Planning Tips With the eclipse now only days away, experienced eclipse chasers are closely watching updated weather forecasts before making final decisions. Because observers will be looking through hundreds of miles of atmosphere near the horizon, distant cloud cover to the northwest may matter more than conditions directly overhead. Useful planning resources include The Eclipse App, SunsetAtlas, Eclipse Horizon , Instituto Geográfico Nacional and TPE, all of which can help confirm sightlines and viewing geometry before eclipse day. WHO WILL See The 2026 Total Solar Eclipse? The Aug. 12 total solar eclipse offers three very different viewing destinations, each with its own advantages and challenges. - Eastern Greenland’s remote Scoresby Sound promises one of the world’s most dramatic eclipse settings, with towering icebergs, Arctic wilderness and relatively reliable weather. Expedition cruise ships packed with eclipse chasers will position themselves within the path of totality. - In Iceland, totality crosses the country’s west coast, bringing the eclipse within easy reach of visitors. Reykjavík, Snæfellsjökull National Park and the Blue Lagoon all lie close to or within the path, while Hellissandur will host the Iceland Eclipse Festival near the point of greatest eclipse. - Spain is expected to attract by far the largest crowds. The path of totality crosses accessible regions including Gijón, A Coruña, Palencia, Burgos, Segovia, Soria, Zaragoza and Mallorca in the Balearic Islands. Northern Spain offers some of the best weather prospects anywhere along the eclipse path.

item.title: Your Ultimate Guide To The Perseid Meteor Shower Peak This Week
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.44
Topline The Perseid meteor shower, one of the year’s celestial highlights, reaches its peak this week beneath perfectly dark skies, promising one of the finest displays of “shooting stars” for years. Thanks to a new moon — which will cause a rare total solar eclipse earlier the same day for parts of Europe, and a partial eclipse in parts of North America — Aug. 12 could become one of the most memorable dates on the 2026 astronomy calendar. Key Facts The Perseids peak overnight on Aug. 12-13 beneath a new moon, creating ideal viewing conditions. The famous meteor shower runs from July 17 to Aug. 24, according to the American Meteor Society Under dark skies, observers could see 60 to 100 meteors per hour, including some bright fireballs. However, for those kinds of numbers, the observer needs to be under a dark rural sky. The best viewing is generally after midnight, when Earth rotates into debris left by Comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle. No telescope is required — just dark skies and patience. A partial solar eclipse will be visible earlier in the day from eastern Canada and parts of the northeastern U.S., while a total solar eclipse crosses eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain. Much of Europe will see a deep partial solar eclipse. Why 2026 Could Be The Best Perseids In Years The Perseids are the Northern Hemisphere’s best-known meteor shower because they arrive during warm summer nights and regularly produce bright, fast meteors and spectacular fireballs. This year, however, astronomers have another reason to be excited. The shower peaks immediately after the Aug. 12 new moon, meaning there will be virtually no moonlight to wash out fainter meteors. Under genuinely dark skies, observers could see as many as 100 meteors per hour as tiny fragments of Comet Swift-Tuttle burn up in Earth’s atmosphere at around 37 miles per second, according to the American Meteor Society Perseid Meteor Shower 2026: Where The Best Viewing Will Be Unlike a solar eclipse, the Perseids don’t require you to be in exactly the right place. Anyone beneath a clear, dark sky can enjoy the display, though the farther you are from city lights, the more meteors you’ll see. Some of the best U.S. locations are International Dark Sky Parks, including Cherry Springs State Park (Pennsylvania), Acadia National Park (Maine), Headlands International Dark Sky Park (Michigan), Bryce Canyon National Park (Utah), Great Basin National Park (Nevada), Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park (Colorado), Big Bend National Park (Texas), Death Valley National Park (California), Grand Canyon National Park (Arizona) and Chaco Culture National Historical Park (New Mexico). However, if you’re planning to camp, book well ahead. The Perseids are the year’s most popular meteor shower, and campsites at many of these destinations are often reserved months in advance. For somewhere closer to home, check a light pollution map and head to an area that looks dark. Partial Solar Eclipse 2026: What North Americans Will See In the U.S., the farther northeast you are, the bigger the partial eclipse you’ll see. Maine gets the deepest eclipse in the contiguous U.S., with Presque Isle seeing about 28% of the sun covered at 1:50 p.m. EDT and Bangor seeing about 23% at 1:53 p.m. EDT. Meanwhile, Boston will see about 16% at 1:55 p.m. EDT, while New York City will see about 10% at 1:54 p.m. EDT. Alaska gets arguably the best U.S. view, with Fairbanks seeing about 37% of the sun covered at 8:27 a.m. AKDT. The biggest partial eclipse in North America will be seen from far northern Canada, with Iqaluit in Nunavut seeing about 61% of the sun blocked by the moon at 1:24 p.m. EDT. In even more remote parts of Nunavut near Greenland, the eclipse will be much deeper. Atlantic Canada also gets a terrific view. St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, will see about 53% of the sun covered at 3:34 p.m. NDT, while Halifax, Nova Scotia, gets about 31% at 3:00 p.m. ADT.

item.title: Puerto Rico’s New $2.5 Billion Resort Community, Psychedelic Retreats And Other Travel News

Puerto Rico Is Building A $2.5 Billion Resort Community Earlier this month Puerto Rico authorized the construction of a $2.5 billion resort community on the southwest coast designed to operate independently from the island’s power and water systems. Forbes Travel Guide’s 2026 Edge List You don’t have to be Odysseus to understand that life-changing travel isn’t about checking off destinations—it’s about committing to the journey. Travel Wise With private jet travel on the rise, many first-time fliers are taking off without knowing exactly what they’re booking. When you reserve a seat on a commercial carrier, somebody has already vetted that airline, the plane and the pilots. Book a private flight and that work is yours: figuring out which way to buy, who’s flying you and whether the trip is worth it at all. Here’s what you need to know before booking a private jet. Because of the therapeutic nature of these retreats, there are plenty of important questions travelers should ask before booking—including the medical protocols and what kind of facilitators and therapists are available to guests. Here’s how to choose the right psychedelic retreat. Passport will be on vacation next week. The newsletter will return tan, rested and ready on August 28. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: Forbes Travel Guide’s Most Beautiful Places In Spain
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.17
Spain’s beauty extends far beyond the famous cities and crowded beaches that dominate most vacation itineraries. From ancient bridges carved into the cliffside to volcanic islands that look like Mars, this diverse country rewards travelers who venture off the well-trodden paths. Stretching from the Cantabrian peaks in the north to the desert landscapes of Andalusia, Spain offers landscapes and experiences that will leave you breathless. You’ll find everything from remote mountain villages to Atlantic islands where visitor numbers are capped per day. Here are some of the most beautiful places in Spain to inspire your next trip. Cudillero, Asturias This colorful fishing village spills down the cliffside in houses painted bright blue, yellow and red. Traditional fishing boats still operate from the tiny harbor, while narrow cobbled streets twist between flower-filled balconies that preserve the village’s traditional charm. Take a walking tour through its backstreets and enjoy the view from the top. The surrounding Green Coast stretches for miles with cliffs, tucked-away beaches reachable only by foot, and coastal meadows where cattle graze within sight of the Cantabrian Sea. Time your visit to coincide with lunch or dinner, when the harbor comes alive with waterfront restaurants setting up, and dine at Restaurante El Faro, Los Arcos or Casa Julio for the day’s catch. Ronda, Andalusia Perched above the 390-foot-deep El Tajo gorge, Ronda is a mountaintop city in Málaga. The 18th-century Puente Nuevo bridge connects the historic Moorish old town with the newer quarter, El Mercadillo, its 320-foot stone arches seeming to grow from the cliff face itself. Views from the bridge span endless Andalusian countryside, while the gorge was carved by the Guadalevín River over millennia. Visitors can descend the steep walking trail into the deep valley for photos of the bridge towering overhead. Cadaqués, Costa Brava Idyllic Cadaqués sits at the end of a mountain road with 120 hairpin turns — a journey that kept this whitewashed fishing village isolated for centuries. Salvador Dalí spent childhood summers here and later made it his home, transforming fishermen’s huts at nearby Port Lligat into his surreal house-museum. Visitors will notice a plaque in town stating that Picasso also lived here, as it is said the famous Spanish artist spent a summer in Cadaqués while working on his Cubist works. The village population of 2,750 swells to 10 times that in summer yet retains its timeless charm. Cozy plazas house family-run restaurants like Casa Nun, and the streets are lined with galleries and clothing boutiques. Hidden coves around Cap de Creus Natural Park offer swimming spots accessible only by winding coastal paths. Picos de Europa, Asturias Rising close to nine miles from the sea, these limestone peaks reach over 8,500 feet, creating one of Europe’s most vertical landscapes. The famous Cares Gorge trail follows narrow ledges carved into cliffsides, providing spectacular vistas. Below, the river cuts through rock hundreds of feet down, while above, jagged peaks catch the light. Take the Fuente Dé cable car to nearly 6,100 feet for easy access to high-altitude hiking trails or tackle the full 7.5-mile Cares Gorge walk that connects Poncebos to Caín Village. Cabo de Gata Natural Park, Andalusia Europe’s only hot desert unfolds across 170 square miles of volcanic coastline, where beaches lie tucked between black lava cliffs. Los Genoveses stretches three quarters of a mile of dark golden sand with not a single building in sight, while Monsul Beach — famous for its appearance in an Indiana Jones film — showcases sculpted rock formations rising directly from turquoise waters. Thousands of flamingos create pink clouds above the salt flats at Las Salinas and more than 1,000 plant species bloom across landscapes that shift from Mediterranean desert to subtropical coast within a few miles. Rent a car to explore the unmarked dirt roads leading to secret coves like Cala de Enmedio or join a kayak tour from San José to reach beaches accessible only from the sea. Teide National Park, Tenerife Spain’s highest peak at 12,200 feet springs from the approximate nine-mile-wide Las Cañadas caldera, formed by volcanic collapses over millions of years. The Roques de García’s towering rock formations shoot up from the crater floor like cathedral spires, while pumice fields stretch to every horizon. Cable car access reaches 11,660 feet, and summit permits allow the final climb to Spain’s highest point. Above 6,500 feet, bizarre formations and clarity of light create otherworldly landscapes. Book the cable car for late afternoon to watch sunset light up the volcanic landscape or get permits for the pre-dawn hike to see sunrise from the summit. Es Vedrà, Ibiza This 1,350-foot limestone monolith juts out of the turquoise waters 1.5 miles off Ibiza’s coast. The uninhabited island has inspired countless legends, with locals claiming it’s the tip of Atlantis or the third most magnetic place on Earth. The perfect triangular silhouette creates one of the Mediterranean’s most photographed scenes, especially from Cala d’Hort beach, where seafood restaurants offer front-row seats to the daily sunset show. Arrive at Cala d’Hort well before sunset to secure a beachfront table at Es Boldado restaurant for grilled fish, sangria and an unobstructed view of the mysterious island. Cíes Islands, Galicia These three uninhabited islands off Vigo cap visitor numbers — 1,800 per day from mid-May to mid-September, dropping to between 250 and 450 per day the rest of the year. Rodas Beach ranks among the world’s finest, with powder-white sand and turquoise Atlantic waters. Hiking trails connect hidden coves, lighthouse viewpoints and archaeological remains. The unique microclimate creates Mediterranean vegetation despite the Atlantic location. Ferry bookings sell out quickly in summer, so reserve tickets online months ahead for July and August visits. Once you arrive, follow the marked trail to the lighthouse at Faro de Cíes for panoramic views over the Galician coast and the open Atlantic. Frigiliana, Andalusia Widely considered one of Spain’s most beautiful villages, Frigiliana is a hillside town of whitewashed houses and winding cobblestone streets. Narrow alleys curve between homes draped in purple bougainvillea, while small shops sell handmade pottery and woven baskets. Moorish irrigation channels still carry mountain water, feeding terraced gardens of oranges and almonds. From rooftop terraces, the view stretches across the valley to the Mediterranean. Take the historic mosaic trail through the old quarter that tells the story of the 1569 Moorish rebellion, ending at the viewpoint overlooking the coastal plains. Sa Calobra, Mallorca Accessible only via one of Europe’s most winding mountain roads, the small cove and hamlet of Sa Calobra hides at the base of the Serra de Tramuntana mountains. The serpentine route descends through hairpin bends and rock tunnels, making driving part of the adventure. The Torrent de Pareis gorge opens into a pebble beach surrounded by 1,000-foot limestone cliffs. The gorge forms a natural amphitheater where classical concerts echo off canyon walls each July. Drive the famously sharp road in the early morning to avoid tour buses, then scramble through the rock tunnel that opens onto the secret beach surrounded by towering rock walls. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: Solar Eclipse And Perseids Peak: What Time To Watch In U.S. And Canada
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.03
Topline Skywatchers across the U.S. and Canada have two celestial events to catch within 24 hours. On Wednesday, Aug. 12, a partial solar eclipse will be visible across much of North America as a total solar eclipse sweeps across Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Then, after darkness falls, the annual Perseid meteor shower will peak beneath perfectly moonless skies. It brings together two of the celestial highlights of summer. Here’s exactly when to look up, where to get the best views and how to watch both safely. Key Facts A partial solar eclipse will be visible across Alaska, 26 U.S. states and every Canadian province and territory on Wednesday, Aug. 12. The deepest eclipse in the contiguous U.S. will be seen from northern Maine, where the moon will cover up to 28% of the sun. Canada gets a much better show, with Nunavut seeing up to 61% obscuration and Newfoundland and Labrador more than 50%. Anyone watching the eclipse must wear ISO 12312-2-certified eclipse glasses at all times. Binoculars, cameras and telescopes require securely fitted solar filters over the front of the optics. Just hours after the eclipse ends, the annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak beneath almost perfectly moonless skies. Between about 2:00 and 4:00 a.m. local time on Thursday, Aug. 13, observers under dark skies could see 60 to 100 meteors per hour, including bright fireballs. However, some “shooting stars” will also be seen before midnight. When And Where To Watch The Partial Solar Eclipse: North America Although North America misses totality, millions of people will still see the moon take a noticeable bite out of the sun. The farther northeast in the U.S., the deeper the eclipse. Alaska also gets an excellent view, while eastern Canada enjoys the deepest partial eclipse anywhere on the continent. When And Where To Watch The Partial Solar Eclipse: U.S. Across the contiguous U.S., the partial solar eclipse begins at 10:27 a.m. MDT in Montana and North Dakota. It ends at 2:52 p.m. EDT in Maine, with the deepest eclipse visible across northern New England. Only a handful of U.S. cities will experience a partial eclipse of about 10% or greater, enough to make the event obvious through eclipse glasses. Here are some of those cities, including how much of the sun will be eclipsed at the peak of the event (and the time of the peak): - Fairbanks, Alaska — 37% (8:27 a.m. AKDT) - Anchorage, Alaska — 28% (8:18 a.m. AKDT) - Presque Isle, Maine — 28% (1:50 p.m. EDT) - Bangor, Maine — 23% (1:53 p.m. EDT) - Portland, Maine — 19% (1:53 p.m. EDT) - Augusta, Maine — 18% (1:52 p.m. EDT) - Montpelier, Vermont — 17% (1:49 p.m. EDT) - Manchester, New Hampshire — 16% (1:53 p.m. EDT) - Boston, Massachusetts — 16% (1:55 p.m. EDT) - Providence, Rhode Island — 15% (1:55 p.m. EDT) - Albany, New York — 13% (1:47 p.m. EDT) - New Haven, Connecticut — 12% (1:54 p.m. EDT) - New York City — about 10% (1:54 p.m. EDT) When And Where To Watch The Partial Solar Eclipse: Canada Every Canadian province and territory will see at least part of the Aug. 12 partial solar eclipse. The event begins in western Canada shortly after 8:30 a.m. local time and continues into the late afternoon in Atlantic Canada, ending in Newfoundland and Labrador at 4:38 p.m. NDT. The deepest views will be in Nunavut and eastern Canada. Here are some notable places in Canada that will see the eclipse, including how much of the sun will be eclipsed at the peak of the event (and the time of the peak): - Iqaluit, Nunavut — 61% (1:24 p.m. EDT) - St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador — 53% (3:34 p.m. NDT) - Moncton, New Brunswick — 32% (2:55 p.m. ADT) - Halifax, Nova Scotia — 31% (3:00 p.m. ADT) - Churchill, Manitoba — 27% (12:02 p.m. CDT) - Québec City — 24% (1:46 p.m. EDT) - Whitehorse, Yukon — 23% (9:26 a.m. MST) - Montréal — 18% (1:45 p.m. EDT) - Ottawa — 15% (1:42 p.m. EDT) When To Watch The Perseids In The U.S. And Canada The second event begins after dark. The Perseids peak overnight on Aug. 12–13 beneath one of the darkest skies in years. Under clear, rural skies, observers could see 60 to 100 meteors per hour, with activity building after midnight and peaking about 2:00 a.m. local time (i.e., the middle of the night). The meteors are tiny fragments shed by Comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle that burn up in Earth’s atmosphere at about 37 miles (59 kilometers) per second. Although they appear to radiate from the constellation Perseus, they can streak across any part of the sky. For the best experience, head somewhere away from city lights, allow your eyes 20 to 30 minutes to adapt naturally to the darkness and look up. No telescope or binoculars are required. When And Where Is The Total Solar Eclipse? The Aug. 12 solar eclipse is total only from a narrow path across eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain, where the moon completely covers the sun for up to 2 minutes 18 seconds. Millions more across Europe will see a deep partial eclipse, with about 91% of the sun covered in London, 92% in Paris, 85% in Berlin and 87% in Vienna. North America lies outside the path of totality, but the moon’s outer shadow still sweeps across much of Canada, Alaska and the northeastern U.S., producing a partial eclipse. When Is The Next Total Solar Eclipse In The U.S? The next total solar eclipse visible from the U.S. will occur on March 30, 2033, when totality crosses northern Alaska, including Nome, where the eclipsed sun will hang low above the horizon, and totality will last about two and a half minutes. The next total eclipse to reach the contiguous U.S. comes on Aug. 23, 2044, crossing parts of Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota before continuing into Canada. Just under a year later, on Aug. 12, 2045, a much broader eclipse will sweep from California to Florida, bringing up to about six minutes of totality across the central U.S.

item.title: UNESCO Just Added 25 New World Heritage Sites—Here’s Where To Go
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.03
Every year, UNESCO adds a new crop of places to its World Heritage List, recognizing landscapes, cities, archaeological sites, and cultural landmarks deemed to have “outstanding universal value.” Some are already household names. Others are places even well-traveled people may have never heard of. This year's additions fall firmly into both camps. At its latest meeting, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee added 25 new properties to the list: 19 cultural sites, five natural sites, and one that combines the two. Among them are places travelers have been visiting for decades, including the D-Day beaches of Normandy, Greece’s Mount Olympus, and the blue-and-white Tunisian village of Sidi Bou Saïd. But there are also plenty of places that may be less familiar: the ancient Xiongnu burial grounds of Mongolia, the elaborate theaters built in the Amazon during Brazil’s rubber boom, and the archaeological remains of Jingdezhen, the Chinese city whose kilns helped shape the global porcelain trade. This year's class also brings three countries onto the World Heritage List for the first time. Comoros earned its inaugural inscription for the Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros, a collection of centuries-old trading towns shaped by the cultures that moved across the Indian Ocean. São Tomé and Príncipe joined the list with the Roças of São Tomé and Príncipe, former colonial agricultural estates that preserve the difficult history of plantation agriculture and forced migration. And South Sudan's first World Heritage site, the Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape, protects a vast sweep of savanna, wetlands, and floodplains crossed by one of the world's largest terrestrial mammal migrations. The United States also gained a new natural World Heritage site with Georgia's Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge. For travelers, the new class offers plenty of reasons to start looking at the map, whether it's to explore the medieval Alamut fortresses of Iran, see the rock-cut mosques and sacred landscapes of Kazakhstan's Mangystau region, or dive among the coral reefs of Jordan's Aqaba Marine Reserve. Here are some of the most compelling new World Heritage sites to visit. Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, United States Tea-colored waterways wind between cypress trees and floating islands in Georgia’s Okefenokee, a more than 400,000-acre refuge that’s home to alligators, black bears, sandhill cranes, and hundreds of bird species. The swamp is one of the largest blackwater wetland ecosystems in North America, and UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List for both its biodiversity and the natural forces—particularly water and fire—that continually reshape its peatlands, forests, lakes, and wetlands. The best way to see it is from the water. Visitors can take guided boat tours or paddle miles of marked canoe and kayak trails from several entrances around the refuge. For a deeper trip, reserve one of the wilderness canoe routes, which can take several days and include nights on raised camping platforms in the swamp. Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara, Japan Before Nara and Kyoto, there were Asuka and Fujiwara. Set among the rice paddies and low hills south of Nara, the former capitals were at the center of enormous political and cultural change between the late sixth and early eighth centuries, as Buddhism spread and Japan developed a centralized system of government. UNESCO's new designation encompasses 19 sites, including palace ruins, Buddhist temples, monumental tombs, and the remains of Fujiwara-kyo, Japan's first capital laid out on a large-scale grid. Together, they document a formative period that helped shape the country for centuries to come. Asuka is about an hour from Nara or Kyoto by train, making it possible to visit as a day trip. Once there, rent a bike to pedal between tombs, temple sites, villages, and rice fields; buses connect many of the major sites as well. Aalto Works, Finland Finland's newest World Heritage site doubles as the blueprint for an architecture road trip. Aalto Works brings together 13 buildings and complexes associated with Alvar Aalto, Aino Marsio-Aalto, Elissa Aalto, and their collaborators, spanning more than half a century of Finnish modernism. The collection ranges from Paimio Sanatorium and the red-brick Säynätsalo Town Hall to Finlandia Hall and the Aalto House in Helsinki. UNESCO recognized the group for its distinctly Finnish take on the Modern Movement, particularly its human-centered approach and use of local materials and surrounding landscapes. Several of the sites are in Helsinki, including the Aalto House and Studio Aalto, both of which can be visited only on guided tours. Advance reservations are recommended. The Wider Area of Mount Olympus, Greece Mount Olympus has been famous for a few thousand years, but its new UNESCO designation goes well beyond its reputation as the mythological home of Zeus and the Greek gods. Rising from near the Aegean coast to 9,573-foot Mytikas, Greece’s highest peak, the mountain encompasses forests, ravines, limestone cliffs, and alpine habitat with unusually rich plant diversity. The property also includes Dion, the ancient Macedonian sanctuary at the mountain's base. UNESCO added the area as a mixed cultural and natural site, recognizing both its biodiversity and geological features and its enduring influence on mythology, art, and literature. Litochoro, about 55 miles from Thessaloniki, is the main jumping-off point. From there, travelers can take short walks through Enipeas Gorge or tackle multi-day routes into the high country. Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites, China Jingdezhen has been producing porcelain for more than 1,000 years, sending its wares from southeastern China to imperial courts and, eventually, markets around the world. Its influence was so great that the city's name became virtually synonymous with fine Chinese porcelain. The new World Heritage property brings together five areas associated with the industry, including kilns, workshops, raw-material extraction sites, transportation routes, and the remains of the Imperial Kiln. UNESCO recognized both the technical advances developed here and Jingdezhen's enormous influence on ceramics production, design, and global trade. Porcelain is still very much a living industry in the city. Travelers can explore historic kiln sites, browse ceramics markets, visit working studios, and even try making their own. Start at the Jingdezhen Imperial Kiln Museum, built around the remains of Ming- and Qing-era imperial kilns, before heading into the city’s contemporary studio and workshop districts. The full list of 25 new UNESCO sites Here’s the complete list of new UNESCO additions in 2026: - Aalto Works, Finland - Beaches of the D-Day Landings, Normandy, 1944, France - The wider area of Mount Olympus, Greece - Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, USA - Alamūt Castle and Related Fortifications, Iran - Amazonia Theaters, Brazil - Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath, India - Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara, Japan - Aqaba Marine Reserve, Jordan - Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape, South Sudan - The Bony Fish Fossils of the Western Limfjord, Denmark - The Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility, Mongolia - Gdynia Modernist City Centre, Poland - Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites, China - The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros, Comoros - Mount Amel Castles, Lebanon - The Roças of Sao Tome and Principe, Sao Tome and Principe - Rock Mosques and Associated Sacred Sites of Mangystau, Kazakhstan - Royal Capetian Fortresses of Languedoc, France - Sebastia, State of Palestine - The System of Italian-style Condominio Theatres, Italy - Tashkent Modernist Architecture, Uzbekistan - Village of Sidi Bou Saïd, Tunisia - Wadi Wurayah, United Arab Emirates - Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Thailand

item.title: A Golden Age Of Total Solar Eclipses Begins Tomorrow
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.00
Topline On Wednesday, Aug. 12, the moon’s central shadow will cross Greenland, Iceland and Spain, beginning one of the most remarkable periods for eclipse enthusiasts in modern history. Over the next 710 days, Earth will experience three total solar eclipses visible from Europe, Africa and Australia, giving travelers an unusually accessible chance to witness one of nature’s rarest spectacles. It makes 2026 through 2028 an extraordinary period for eclipse chasers and anyone who ever wanted to experience a total eclipse of the sun. Key Facts The first event begins tomorrow, Aug. 12, when a total solar eclipse crosses eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain. It will be Europe’s first total solar eclipse since 2015, and mainland Europe’s first since 1999. The centerpiece comes on Aug. 2, 2027, with the so-called “eclipse of the century.” Totality will last up to 6 minutes and 23 seconds near Luxor, Egypt — the longest land-based total solar eclipse between 1991 and 2114. The trilogy concludes on July 22, 2028, when totality sweeps across Australia and New Zealand. Sydney will experience its first total solar eclipse since 1857, while Western Australia will enjoy more than five minutes of totality. The sequence is unusually travel-friendly. Rather than crossing remote oceans, the paths pass through destinations with established tourism infrastructure, including Iceland, Spain, Morocco, Tunisia, Egypt and Australia. Although similar trios of total solar eclipses repeat every 18 years, few have crossed so many accessible and culturally significant destinations. Why This Is A Golden Age Most people consider themselves fortunate to witness a single total solar eclipse during their lifetime. Between tomorrow and July 2028, it will be possible to experience three across three continents, each offering a completely different setting — Arctic landscapes in Greenland and Iceland, ancient monuments in Egypt and the deserts and cities of Australia. Three total solar eclipses within about two years occur because three separate Saros series happen to align over a short period. Similar trios occurred between 1990 and 1992 and again from 2008 to 2010, with the next not arriving until the mid-2040s. Total Solar Eclipse 2026 Tomorrow’s eclipse is arguably Europe’s most important astronomical event in more than a quarter of a century. Totality will cross eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain, offering dramatic low-altitude views of the eclipsed sun above volcanic landscapes, glaciers and medieval cities. Although maximum totality lasts only a little over two minutes, it marks the beginning of an extraordinary era of eclipses. For many European travelers, it will also be the easiest and most accessible opportunity to witness totality for years to come. Total Solar Eclipse 2027 Less than a year later, the event many eclipse chasers have spent years planning takes place. The Aug. 2, 2027 eclipse will produce the longest land-based totality between 1991 and 2114, peaking at 6 minutes and 23 seconds near Luxor in Egypt. Combined with almost guaranteed clear skies across parts of North Africa and a path that crosses ancient temples, Mediterranean coastlines and the Nile Valley, it’s easy to see why it’s already known as the “eclipse of the century.” Few eclipses in modern times have combined such exceptional duration, reliable weather and globally significant cultural landmarks along the path of totality. Total Solar Eclipse 2028 The trilogy concludes in spectacular fashion on July 22, 2028. Totality will sweep across Western Australia before crossing New Zealand, with Sydney witnessing its first total solar eclipse in more than 170 years. Remote parts of the Australian Outback will enjoy more than five minutes of totality beneath some of the clearest skies on Earth. For eclipse chasers, it provides a fitting finale to one of the richest three-year periods for total solar eclipses in recent history.

item.title: When To Cancel Your Summer Vacation Because Of Wildfires
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.99
The list of vacation destinations burning this summer reads like a bucket list itinerary: Bordeaux, Crete, the Aegean coast and Bend, Oregon. Fires across Europe have killed at least 17 civilians, six firefighters and two helicopter crew, and forced roughly 330,000 people from their homes in France and Spain. France has already passed its worst fire year on record and is running at 6.2 times its 20-year average, according to the data research firm Ranking Atlas. If you have a trip booked, you're probably doing arithmetic you didn't expect. Here's where the fires have already forced the call: - Central Oregon. The Akawa Butte fire northeast of Sisters reached 27,491 acres before evacuation notices eased. Visit Central Oregon, the tourism marketing agency, has been promoting a hyperlocal smoke map this summer, partly to prevent unnecessary cancellations in towns that weren't affected. - Spokane, Washington. Three fires broke out around the city on August 1 and are now managed together as the Spokane Area Fires. Roughly 65,000 people have been evacuated, and more than 600 structures were hit. An air quality alert covering 13 eastern Washington counties warned that fine particulate levels could reach the "very unhealthy" range. - Gironde and the Arcachon Basin, France. About 40,000 visitors at 45 campsites in Gironde and the neighboring Landes were evacuated, and the prefect publicly asked tourists to stay away. On the Cap Ferret peninsula, the summer season has been effectively canceled. - Crete and the area west of Athens. Authorities moved about 8,000 residents and tourists out of the coastal resort of Agia Galini, Crete on July 29. The fire that started west of Athens on July 31 destroyed more than 100 homes and drove out over 1,000 people, more than 250 of them evacuated from the beaches by boat. Every one of those flare-ups has travelers asking the same question: Should I cancel, and if so, when? But you won’t find the answer on the TV news. More often than not, it comes down to air quality, whether anyone has ordered an evacuation and how your travel insurance policy defines a disaster. Get that wrong and you'll cancel a trip that didn't need canceling—or forfeit a deposit you can't recover. When Should You Cancel Travel Because Of A Fire? Headlines aren't always enough to prompt a cancellation, according to experts. Daniel Grainger, founder of Ranking Atlas, ran a country-level analysis of the European Union's fire records. He says cancellation decisions are based on a specific destination's fire trend rather than this week's news. He points out that in Portugal, wildfires have burned the equivalent of 23% of the country's land area over 20 years, yet this year's fire activity is running at only 0.35 percent of the seasonal average. Most Mediterranean coastlines see some fire activity every August. Karen Clay, professor of economics and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University, says the common error is treating one number as the whole story. "The air quality index can worsen by 100 points across a short distance as smoke plumes move," she says. Those index categories are built around healthy adults, she adds, so anyone with asthma, heart disease, a pregnancy or a young child needs to react sooner. She also points out that people check the forecast the week before instead of the morning of, which is when advisories and smoke shift. The index itself is slipperier than travelers assume. Colleen Rosales, strategic partnerships director at OpenAQ, a nonprofit that publishes open air quality data, says air quality indices are calculations rather than physical readings, and countries build their own to match their own health standards. A fine particulate concentration that reads "good" in Mongolia can read "moderate" in the U.S. Providers don't always disclose how they got their number. Air quality indices don't mean the same thing everywhere. Also, a fire in one part of town doesn’t mean the entire destination is closed. My U.S. home base is in Spokane, and the fires there illustrate this point. Nearly half the city’s neighborhoods were evacuated or at risk. The images were terrible. But Visit Spokane’s latest advisory says the region remains open to visitors, with many events and attractions continuing as scheduled. Hotels are taking reservations. Several are discounting rooms for evacuees and first responders. Bottom line: A fire in the news doesn't necessarily mean the destination has stopped functioning, or isn't open for business. Does Travel Insurance Cover Wildfire Cancellations? "When severe weather or a natural disaster causes an extended delay so your travel carrier can’t get you to your destination for at least 24 hours from your original scheduled arrival, that can be a covered reason for trip cancellation," says Daniel Durazo, director of external communications at Allianz Partners USA. "To travel insurers, a heat wave, smoke or a bad forecast alone are not covered reasons for cancellation. Yet widespread evacuations, destroyed accommodations or an official order preventing access can change the equation." Durazo says the wildfires near Bordeaux were a clear case of a destination becoming uninhabitable rather than simply unpleasant, and that people with travel insurance policies could be reimbursed for unused, prepaid, nonrefundable trip costs, subject to their policy terms. Allianz Partners’ 2026 Global Travel Confidence Index, conducted by Ipsos, found that 68% of American travelers now weigh environmental risks and extreme weather when choosing where to go. Terry Boynton, president of Yonder Travel Insurance, draws the same line. "For heat, wildfire smoke and other extreme weather events, the key question isn't whether the conditions are unpleasant," he says. "It's whether they directly disrupt your travel plans in a way that is covered by your policy." If smoke cancels or badly delays your flight, trip cancellation, trip interruption or travel delay benefits may apply. If you simply decide not to go, they generally don't. Chrissy Valdez, senior director of operations at Squaremouth, says standard trip cancellation coverage on travel insurance policies responds to mandatory evacuation orders, uninhabitable accommodations, airport closures and supplier cancellations. "Where it falls short is when a traveler feels uncomfortable going unless there is an evacuation order or uninhabitable lodging," she explains. "Most standard policies don't treat high temperatures or poor air quality as covered cancellation reasons." In those situations, a more expensive "cancel for any reason" or "interruption for any reason" policy provides more flexibility, she adds. The timing can be tricky. Buy insurance after a fire is burning, and you’ve bought nothing. The U.K. insurer InsureandGo designated the current European wildfires a known event as of July 22. Every carrier sets its own date, and once it passes, that fire is no longer an unforeseen event on any policy sold afterward. There’s also a category of disruption nobody’s policy addresses. Nick Cavanaugh, CEO of Sensible Weather and a climate scientist, says traditional coverage is built for low-frequency, high-severity events. Smoke and heat tend to ruin the trip without canceling it. His company's survey of 600 U.S. leisure travelers found 78% have had a trip negatively affected by bad weather. That gap between what people assume is covered and what's listed in the policy can be frustrating, according to Joe Cronin, president of International Citizens Insurance. But some gaps are wider than others. "Travel medical coverage generally does apply if you go anyway and end up needing treatment for heat exhaustion or respiratory issues," he says. Do Hotels And Vacation Rentals Offer Wildfire Refunds? Here you have more leverage than you think, at least in some places. If your hotel, campsite or rental is evacuated by local authorities, French law treats it as force majeure, and the provider is generally required to refund the unused portion of the stay. Under EU package travel rules, travelers who booked a package can cancel before departure when unavoidable and extraordinary circumstances hit at or near the destination, with a full refund and no additional compensation. The platforms moved during the Gironde fires. Airbnb told the French newspaper la Voix du Nord that it extended the scope of its policy to cover the entire Gironde region in light of local advice against traveling there. Many suppliers waived cancellation fees, even on nonrefundable rates, when access was impossible or a property had closed. SNCF, the French railway system, allowed free changes and cancellations on trips to Gironde and Landes. Pay attention to the fine print. Airbnb's Major Disruptive Events Policy covers unforeseeable natural disasters and severe weather, plus mandatory government evacuation orders. Weather common enough to be foreseeable in a given location is usually excluded. For example, during the January 2025 Los Angeles fires, one guest with a rental near Pacific Palisades was told her cancellation didn't qualify. Ask for everything in writing, too. Keep the evacuation order or prefectural notice, and enclose it with any request for a refund or rebooking. Suppliers with no legal obligation to refund will often move a booking rather than lose the customer, and Sensible Weather's Cavanaugh says booking direct rather than through a third party usually buys you a real person to ask. How To Plan A Trip During Wildfire Season The season isn’t finished. Above-normal significant fire potential continues this month in much of the Northwest, northeast California, the northern Great Basin and the West Slope. Washington has already seen more than 1,000 fires burn about 425,000 acres this year, the most since 2021, according to the state Department of Natural Resources. Experienced travelers aren't panicking, though. "Despite another summer marked by record-breaking temperatures and increasingly severe weather events worldwide, most experienced international travelers are not overly concerned about extreme heat or weather-related health risks when planning trips abroad," says Bill McIntyre, a director at Global Rescue. Its survey found only 12% are "extremely or very concerned," with 52% "somewhat or slightly concerned." What distinguishes them is preparation. "Experienced international travelers understand that unpredictable weather is one of many travel risks that can be managed with preparation," says Jeff Weinstein, a paramedic and medical operations manager for Global Rescue. "They recognize that staying hydrated, adjusting itineraries and understanding local conditions will significantly reduce the likelihood of heat-related illness." Weinstein says their real concern isn't avoiding every risk. It's knowing they'll have access to quality medical care and, if necessary, medical evacuation. Check your destination against its own seasonal average rather than the country's latest news headlines. Take a look at the local air quality reading the morning of your departure. Ask your lodging about air conditioning, filtration and backup power. Build in a buffer day. Book rentals or hotels with flexible refund policies, which costs less than a "cancel for any reason" rider and pays out faster. Remember, canceling your vacation is the only decision here you can't reverse. Smoke will eventually clear—and maybe soon—but a forfeited deposit stays forfeited. So this summer, make the call as late as your refund window allows.

item.title: Global UHNWs Compete To Book Expensive Suites, Lodges And Experiences
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.90
The controversy between YouTube travel reviewer Ryan Walker and Amanvari highlighted one point everyone can agree on. Hotel rates are through the roof. The newest property for the uber-luxury Aman Resorts group was charging $6,000 per night during its opening week, a period when most hotels heavily discount rates as they work out the kinks and because not all facilities may yet be open. Andrea Grisdale, the CEO of IC Bellagio, a firm that organizes private access experiences in Italy, says one wealthy client recently told her, "I want to stay in the hotel, not buy it." Data from the Virtuoso travel network shows an average nightly rate of $1,983 for bookings in June. That's double pre-COVID levels. Grisdale says that since the surge in "revenge travel" post-COVID, some seasonal properties in Italy now remain open through early January rather than closing in November to accommodate increased demand at the top end of the market. However, if you are looking to save a few bucks by traveling in the shoulder season, look again. "Fall is the new summer," says Misty Belles, Virtuoso’s vice president of global communications, noting that sales for September through November are currently tracking 69% ahead of last year. Festive season bookings are up 65% year-over-year. And don’t blink, or you may find yourself having to move to Plan B. Future bookings for trips one or more years in advance that cost more than $100,000 are up 49%. The rush to pay top dollar, rupiah, yuan, euro, etc., for vacations as far out as 2028 is Econ 101. David Kolner, an executive vice president with Virtuoso, whose member agencies sold over $35 billion in luxe trips in 2025, says demand for plush and posh accommodations is more global than in the past. Super-rich clients in the U.S. are now competing with UHNW families from around the world for that presidential suite, exclusive residence, or safari lodge takeover. What’s more, many of the hot properties are small. Twenty-five percent of the group’s preferred properties have fewer than 50 rooms, so while the United States still rules in terms of super-rich population, wealthy families from the rest of the world have also caught the travel bug and are going both on and off the beaten path. It’s not cheap, even for entry-level accommodations in popular destinations. On Lake Como, starting prices at Grand Hotel Tremezzo begin at around 1,800 euros plus VAT, while 24-room Passalacqua is 2,800 euros, plus VAT. For six-bedroom Villa Sola Cabiati you will pay 20,000 euros per night plus VAT. Families take the villa for three or four weeks, says Managing Director Silvio Vettorello, using it as a base and then hopping around Europe. As with the villa being a one-of-a-kind, Vettorello says the hotels' signature suites are also unique, with many already booked for next summer. He says if you want a specific suite, or a suite with a connecting room, now is the time to book. Virtuoso travel advisors say 70% of clients are willing to pay more for unique or exclusive accommodations. Millennials who are benefiting from inheriting $84 trillion, according to Cerulli Associates, are apparently anxious to transfer that wealth, with 67% of advisors saying the thirst for travel is being driven by "new luxury products and experiences." Across all age groups, advisors say clients are prioritizing bucket list and once-in-a-lifetime trips, again meaning that, despite some hemming and hawing, there is minimal resistance to paying at the top of the market. Discover Puerto Rico CEO Jorge L. Perez says, "We haven’t seen any pushback," noting occupancy in the island’s luxury properties hovers just below 90% year-round. The same goes for Karen Whitt, a vice president at Hartling Group in Turks & Caicos, whose properties include Sands Grace Bay, Palms Grace Bay and Shore Club Grace Bay. In recent years, Providenciales International Airport has expanded its facilities for private jets. Visit Los Cabos Managing Director Rodrigo Esponda says occupancy and prices for signature suites and villas are as strong as ever. Singapore Tourist Board Vice President Dawn Ng adds, "The wealthy are trading up to bigger suites. They don't see hotels anymore as just a place to sleep. They see them as an extension of their lifestyle." She points to AP House by Swiss watchmaker Audemars Piguet, which opened in the historic Raffles Hotel's Bar and Billiard Room. Many of its timepieces run into the six figures. Others worry that the continued push to raise rates could backfire if consumers see it as a money grab. Grisdale says that while high flyers are sympathetic to cost increases for suppliers, including labor costs, they want to see tangible improvements in the places they stay. Vettorello says his group has a policy of refurbishing all rooms every three years, particularly updating technology such as the charger ports used for mobile devices. Barbara Muckermann, Group CEO of Kempinski, which both owns and manages luxury hotels, says the industry has a "creativity problem" similar to fashion's. If it doesn't change, it risks a falloff. She says hotels are "no longer a refuge from the city, but the gateway into it." It is launching E.R.A. at its hotels in Munich and Prague, short for experience real access. Each hotel will include a resident curator, and initial experiences include a morning run with Lothar Matthäus, who guided Germany to a World Cup title in 1990, and a helicopter ride over five royal castles with the private historian of the Wittelsbachs, the house that ruled Bavaria for 738 years. Blue Parallel President Emmanuel Burgio agrees that travel providers need to do more than increase rates to maintain momentum. A specialist in custom luxury travel in Latin America, Burgio says the average spend per trip is $100,000, and that it's not price but time that is the biggest constraint. Following the trend of luxury private jet experiences that use VIP airliners for 50 travelers, Blue Parallel is launching custom private jet experiences, where clients can bring their own jets or the company can arrange charter flights. He says UHNWs have "all the tangible items and they are looking to splurge on experiences. Our job is to offer value, which means taking them to places they have never heard of." He points to Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site in northern Brazil that recently opened to tourism, where you can ride ATVs across its dunes and lagoons. Explora Chief Marketing Officer Jacqueline Barney says rates at its lodges in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile and Peru run over $3,000 per night, but are inclusive. "We’re not charging $12 for a bottle of water." There are dozens of experiences available at each lodge that don’t need to be pre-booked, and they are included along with fees for national parks. Nothing is outsourced, she says, so that Explora can control the quality. All guides are employees. Gourmet meals, included as well, feature collaborations with chefs from Michelin-star restaurants. French Side Travel CEO Mark Bonte says even with creativity and product investment, "It's getting to a point where you can't keep doing a 10% price increase every year." He says France is losing high-end clients to Spain, Portugal and Croatia. Bonte says wealthy Americans are either skipping places like Champagne and cutting back their stays in Paris, deciding instead to go a bit off the beaten track to Corsica and France's Basque Country. Southern Crossings Director Paul Groves-Berry says this summer, the winter season in Australia and New Zealand, has seen an influx of Americans and others who were attracted not only by the off-season pricing down under but also by a desire to avoid the record heat and crowding that made headlines in Europe. In a world where there is more competition to grab the best suite or have that lodge reserved exclusively for your group, sometimes more is more. Blue Parallel's Burgio says if the product is intriguing, "People question if it doesn't feel expensive enough." Nubia Tours' Haytham Atwan, whose company specializes in Egypt, says that after years of having its luxury hotels priced "at less than what you would pay for a 3-star hotel in London or New York," that pricing has finally risen to a level where hotel owners can invest back into the properties. "Reducing prices is easy," he says. "Getting them back up takes years and years."

item.title: 7 New UNESCO World Heritage Sites Worth Traveling For In 2026
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.53
In July 2026, UNESCO added 25 new World Heritage Sites (19 cultural, five natural and one mixed) bringing the global list to 1,273 sites across 173 countries. This year’s additions also marked a milestone for Comoros, São Tomé and Príncipe and South Sudan, which gained their first-ever World Heritage Sites. South Sudan entered the list with a natural site, the Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape, which is home to one of the largest known terrestrial mammal migration in the world, with millions of antelope moving across its savannas and wetlands. While South Sudan is among the countries under Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory, here are seven new UNESCO World Heritage Sites that are worth visiting in 2026. Beaches of the D-Day Landings, Normandy, France UNESCO recognized the D-Day beaches in Normandy for their direct association with the Allied landings of June 6, 1944, which marked the beginning of the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi occupation. The site stretches across roughly 50 miles of coastline. It includes five D-Day landing beaches, such as Utah and Omaha, where American troops arrived, as well as Pointe du Hoc, a 110-foot cliff stormed by U.S. Rangers and the American Cemetery at Colleville‑sur‑Mer. Since it lies between Caen and Bayeux, the easiest way to reach it is via direct trains from Paris. Bayeux is particularly convenient for Omaha Beach, Pointe du Hoc and Colleville-sur-Mer. The Wider Area of Mount Olympus, Greece While Mount Olympus combines one of the most recognizable stories in Western mythology, it is also an impressive natural destination. UNESCO highlights not only its association with Zeus and the Twelve Olympian Gods, but also its limestone cliffs, deep gorges, unusual geology and importance as a Mediterranean plant-biodiversity hotspot. Mount Olympus rises in northern Greece, between Macedonia and Thessaly, close to the Aegean coast. Litochoro is the principal gateway for exploring the mountain and is accessible by road and train from Thessaloniki or Athens. Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, U.S. Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is the only U.S. site added to the World Heritage List in 2026. Okefenokee protects the largest lowland freshwater peatland in the world’s subtropical zone. Its total area is 680 square miles, which also contains about 92% of the wider Okefenokee Swamp. Its vast wetlands can be explored by canoe, kayak and boat, offering close encounters with alligators, birds and an ecosystem UNESCO recognizes as globally exceptional. The refuge lies in southeastern Georgia and northeastern Florida, with its main visitor entrance near Folkston, Georgia. Jacksonville is a convenient major-airport gateway city, close to the refuge. Aqaba Marine Reserve, Jordan Aqaba brings a completely different experience to the list: snorkeling and diving in a newly UNESCO-recognized coral ecosystem. UNESCO calls it the world's northernmost tropical coral reef system, with more than 150 hard-coral species and 500 fish species. Its corals have developed unusual resilience to high temperatures and marine heatwaves. The reserve lies along Jordan’s short Red Sea coastline at Aqaba, at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba. Travelers can fly into Amman's Queen Alia International Airport and connect to King Hussein International Airport in Aqaba via domestic flight or reach it by car. Village of Sidi Bou Saïd, Tunisia Sidi Bou Saïd is arguably one of the most visually appealing of the 2026 additions, with whitewashed buildings, vivid blue doors and windows, narrow streets and Mediterranean views. But UNESCO’s rationale goes deeper and stems from a history shaped by Sufi traditions, distinctive architecture, and generations of artists drawn to the village. Sidi Bou Saïd sits on a cliff overlooking the Mediterranean just outside Tunis, next to Carthage. Travelers fly into Tunis-Carthage International Airport and can easily reach the village by taxi or by train. The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros Comoros is a little-known island nation between East Africa and Madagascar with three main islands: Grande Comore (Ngazidja), Anjouan (Ndzuwani) and Mohéli (Mwali). 2026 is the first year a site in Comoros was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage destination. The inscription includes six historic towns: Moroni, Itsandra, Ntsoudjini and Iconi on Grande Comore (Ngazidja), and Mutsamudu and Domoni on Anjouan (Ndzuwani). These medinas trace how settlements dating back at least to the 11th century became sultanate capitals shaped by African, Islamic and Indian Ocean trading networks. International travelers generally enter through Prince Said Ibrahim International Airport near Moroni via Nairobi, Kenya or Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath, India Sarnath is one of Buddhism's most significant sacred places and one of Buddhism's four principal pilgrimage sites with stupas, monasteries, archaeological ruins and living pilgrimage traditions. It is believed to be where Buddha delivered his first sermon after attaining enlightenment in the 6th century BCE. It is also a Buddhist monastic community, or Sangha, that effectively began with his earliest disciples. Sarnath lies just outside Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh, making it particularly easy to add to a northern India itinerary. Lal Bahadur Shastri International Airport in Varanasi is the easiest getaway for international travelers.

item.title: Nantucket’s Greydon House Expands With New Lounge And Suites
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.38
Nantucket may be a tiny island, but the 48-square-mile island just got more space to stay overnight. Greydon House, the 10-year-old boutique hotel in the center of town, just opened a new lounge and four individual guest suites, as part of an ongoing expansion. Connected to the original 1950s era Broad Street property by a brick pathway, the expansion continues Greydon House’s commitment to Nantucket’s architectural legacy. Designed by a Nantucket-based team – Emeritus designers and interiors by Natasha Willauer – the addition includes a ground flour lounge called The Green Room, now open to the public Thursday through Monday from 2 p.m. to 9 p.m. The Green Room’s soft loungers and wraparound 14-seat bar offer an intimate setting for cocktails, light bites, and conversation in a seagreen colored space. Decor and finishings were sourced from local Nantucket antique shops, vintage markets across New England, and independent artisans who crafted on-site furnishings. “The goal was never to replicate the original, but to create something that feels like a natural extension – more like a cousin than a twin,” said Willauer. “We wanted each space to feel individually lived-in, while still connected to the larger story of Greydon House.” The four new guest suites are each unique, and designed to embrace Nantucket’s coastal landscape with soft blues and greens layered with warm woods, brick hues, and brass accents. Some of the suites have Gothic windows overlooking North Water Street and select bathrooms feature dual shower systems, marble finishes, and custom walnut vanities. Set in a former sea captain’s home and originally designed by Roman and Williams, the 20-room Greydon House has become a luxury destination on Nantucket over the past decade. The property is consistently named one of the best hotels on Nantucket and is home to the Venetian restaurant Via Mare. Next up in the expansion is a patio and garden slated for this fall. Visiting Nantucket Nantucket attracts nearly 2 million annual visitors. Despite reports that Nantucket has seen an explosion in tourism, data from the ferry operators and airlines (the only ways to reach the island, which is not connected to land by bridge or in any other way), indicates that tourism rates have remained steady in recent years. Census data shows that Nantucket has a year-round population of about 14,ooo residents, though around 80,000 people reside on the island in July and August. Lodging is a consistent topic of conversation for locals and visitors. The island has fewer than 1,000 standard hotel rooms and strictly regulates short term rentals and secondary platforms, like Airbnb. Nantucket’s Culture and Tourism office offers free referral services for overnight stays and lists vacancies, if available, daily. Hotels rarely open on the island. Most recently, Blue Flag Capital reopened the renovated Beachside Hotel in 2025.

item.title: How To Move Or Retire To Spain
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.23
There are many reasons you might want to move or retire to Spain. Its cities are perennial travel favorites, and its beaches are admired and sought out—it has the most Blue Flag beaches in Europe, those known for their strong environmental credentials. The cost of living in Spain is much lower than it is in many other Western countries, such as the U.S. and France. In Spain, the cost of living for a single person, including rent, is around $731. This is compared to €1,166 in the U.S. and €1,200 in France. And if you’re looking for other reasons, why not believe the expats who already live there? The 13th annual Expat Insider Survey, voted on by the six million expat members of InterNations, found that Spain ranked ninth globally in 2025 and sixth in 2026, across a range of factors. In particular, though, Spain ranked first among all countries for its quality of life in this report, marking its fifth consecutive year in this spot. Expats love its leisure, culture, nightlife, and culinary options. Clearly, the weather plays a part too. In 2026, the consultancy group Resonance ranked Madrid and Barcelona among the top 10 cities in Europe to visit or live in. Global Citizens Solutions, a residency and citizenship planning advisory firm, recently constructed an index to take a look at the most desirable locations for high-net-worth individuals to buy holiday homes. Spain ranks 1st worldwide because it is the only market to combine the second-highest appreciation rate (12.5%) in the top 10 with the highest quality-of-life score in the entire dataset, driven by Mallorca and Ibiza. How To Move To Spain From The U.S. There are various ways to move to Spain depending on your personal situation. If you have a work contract in Spain, the Highly Qualified Professional visa is the route for skilled workers. If you have Spanish ancestry, the citizenship-by-descent route remains open.
