item.title: Leadership Summit 2026: Inspiring Grit and Growth Amid Unprecedented Change
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.31
Share Podcast Leadership Summit 2026: Inspiring Grit and Growth Amid Unprecedented Change A conversation with University of Pennsylvania’s Angela Duckworth on how grit applies in a world of AI. Most leaders are asking the same question about AI: Will it make their teams more productive—or slowly erode the very skills they’re trying to build? In this special episode, as part of the recent HBR Leadership Summit 2026, University of Pennsylvania’s Angela Duckworth says her long-standing research on grit—and the fact the most successful people aren’t simply persistent, they stay committed to long-term goals while adapting their tactics as the world changes—is more relevant than ever in the age of generative AI. Rather than replacing human capability, she explains, AI can become a powerful coach that accelerates learning, if people treat it as something to learn from, not simply something that does the work for them. Duckworth’s new book is Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best. ADI IGNATIUS: Welcome to the HBR IdeaCast. I’m Adi Ignatius. Artificial intelligence promises to make us faster and more productive, but there is an underlying question as to what it means to allow AI to do more of our thinking. What will happen to our ability to learn, to improve, and develop expertise over time? What will happen to our ability to learn, to improve, and to develop expertise over time? Today’s guest argues that the answer depends less on the technology itself and more on how we choose to use it. Angela Duckworth is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and her research has long focused on what separates high achievers from everyone else. Enter: AI. I spoke to her recently as part of the 2026 HBR Leadership Summit about her research that suggests AI can actually accelerate learning when it’s used as a coach rather than a crutch. We’ll also hear about why young workers feel both excited and uneasy about these tools, and we’ll hear practical advice for leaders who want their teams to become more productive and more capable. Duckworth is the author of Grit, as well as of the forthcoming book, Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best. ANGELA DUCKWORTH: As you know, I do study grit, but I want to put grit in the context of AI and I want to cover three questions. One is how grit is integral to becoming excellent at what you do, no matter what it is that you want to do, and how that relates to the second question, which is AI and whether AI helps or hinders grit, and under what circumstances a leader might make AI work for you versus against you. That, of course, is the third question in particular, which is how a leader and a team might optimally use AI to become better at what they do. So to begin, what is the relationship between grit and excellence? Why is grit a necessary, if not sufficient, element to successful leaders, successful individuals in any domain that I have studied? I’m going to give you a little test. So you can take it right now. It’s got four questions on it. And you’re not going to formally score yourself, but these four items are from the grit scale. It’s a questionnaire I developed from interviewing Olympic gold medalists and Nobel Prize winners, world-class achievers across domains. And here’s one item. “I am a hard worker.” If I ask the people who know you best, how many would go out of their way to say that you are an especially hard worker? The more that is true, the higher your grit score. And in particular, the higher your perseverance sub-score, because grit is not just perseverance, but it’s also passion. So let’s start with, “I am a hard worker.” Here’s another perseverance item on the grit scale. “I finish whatever I begin.” High achievers who have grit have a bias toward completion. They hate to quit. They especially hate to quit when things are hard and everybody else is quitting. So these two items index your perseverance for long-term goals. That’s half of grit. Let me show you two other items you can reflect on your own character at the moment. Now, before I show them to you, I need to warn you they are reverse-scored. And by that I mean, when I show you these items, if you say, “Wow, Angela knows me. These are just like me,” you actually get a lower passion sub-score and a lower overall grit score. “I have difficulty maintaining my focus on projects that take more than a few months to complete.” Here’s another reverse-scored passion item. “I often set a goal, but later choose to pursue a different one.” When you ask me about the passion of high achievers, I want to point out that it’s not about intensity. It’s not about pulling all-nighters. It’s not about being an extrovert. It’s not about having manic levels of energy and enthusiasm. Excitement is common, but endurance is rare. The passion of gritty high achievers is consistency. It’s being loyal to some top-level goal that keeps you interested, keeps you committed over long periods of time. And that is why grit is not just perseverance, but passion and perseverance for especially long-term goals. Weeks, months, years, decades, in some cases, a lifetime. Now, this diagram is an X-ray of what goes on in the mind of a very gritty high achiever. They do have a top-level goal. They have an ultimate why that gives meaning and sense and direction to all of their mid-level goals, things I want to accomplish in the next five years or three years. And then you go down, this is, of course, a simplified diagram, but at the very bottom of the hierarchy is your to-do list. The very bottom is what you have to get done today and this week. And here’s where I think you need to be agile, adaptive, and respond to circumstances. So you should be stubborn at the top. Your value shouldn’t change, your mission shouldn’t change, your top-level goal should not change, but very agile at the bottom. And you have to be agile in part because the world is changing. So you want to capitalize on those opportunities, including AI. And all of this keeps you on a learning curve. This is a slide that, stylized fashion, summarizes the research of Anders Ericsson, a cognitive scientist who coined the term the 10,000-hour rule. 10,000 hours of practice. What Anders studied was the learning curves. We have skill on the vertical axis, you have time on the horizontal axis. He studied the learning curves of people who became grand chess masters or prima ballerinas or world-class CEOs. And what he found was that if you can stay on a learning curve and continue to improve, then maybe even more important than talent, he would say that, I would say that, is your ability to consistently work hard, not give up when everyone else is giving up, and actually stay focused on something long enough to get really great at it. And this is why it’s so relevant to AI, because the question that looms I think in everyone’s mind is, will individuals continue to become more excellent themselves or, with an invention that does your thinking for you, will just the opposite happen? I want to share with you data that was collected in collaboration with the Walton Family Foundation and Gallup. This is a nationally representative sample of Gen Z young adults, 18 to 28, about 2,000 of them. And we asked them in late October of last year, “How many of you have used AI in the last month for the following purposes?” And you can see that three out of four young adults have used AI in the last month as of October. That’s probably north of that figure today, which is just a few months later. The number one use is Google or a substitute for Google. Essentially, if you look at this rank ordering, what you see is that Gen Z is using AI primarily to be more productive. You might be alarmed at those numbers at the bottom of the figure, using AI as your girlfriend or boyfriend or as a substitute for a friend or when you’re not supposed to. We can certainly discuss that in the Q&A, but primarily I want to say that Gen Z is leaning in to using ChatGPT, Claude, and other platforms to become more productive. In the same survey, we asked them how they felt about AI use. And there’s a deep ambivalence. They love that it makes them more productive, but they worry, and they worry about the same things that you worry about and that I worry about, which is that if I use AI, it’s like a crutch and it’s going to make me as an individual over the long-term lazier and less smart. And that brings me to the question of, what to do? As a leader, what to do? If we understand that grit keeps you on a learning curve, if we understand that excellence takes a lot of hard work and continuous improvement, but now we have this invention which makes us definitely more productive in the short-term, potentially at long-term cost, what hope is there? And I want to share some research findings that do give me hope. I ran an experiment. This was led by my then graduate student, Benjamin Lira. We randomly assigned individuals to condition, but everybody in the experiment had to rewrite a terrible cover letter. So if you look on this laptop screen, there is this long, oh my God, I don’t want to read it, cover letter to a hiring manager. We gave that to the young adults and others in our study. And we said, “We want you to rewrite it.” But in one condition, you had to do it on your own. In other conditions, you were allowed to use AI to do your work for you. So that would be the simulation of what a lot of people are doing today, which is copying, pasting something into an AI platform like ChatGPT and having, at the press of a button, an instantly rewritten cover letter. And then we had a holdout control that did no practice at all. And I want to share the results. Imagine that you were in this experiment. You either had no practice at all or you had to practice on your own without an AI tool, or finally, you were in the condition where you got the tool. And if you predict the results of this and you are like the people that we sampled in a separate forecasting study, you would predict that over time, the people who use the AI tool would actually maybe write better cover letters in the moment, but on a test, their own writing skill would be diminished. This is the concern that AI makes us lazy and stupid. And what we found, in fact, to our surprise honestly, was that when you see this cover letter that your AI chatbot has produced for you instantly, you actually yourself get better at writing skill, not just immediately, but a day and a week later. So your writing skill has enduringly improved. You are better than practicing on your own. You are also better than the participants who had no practice at all. In other words, improbably, we found that using AI to boost immediate productivity in this case also boosted long-term skill. Not at all what we expected and I think not at all what other people expect. And here is what I think is going on. When you use AI, you may reduce your effort in terms of doing things faster, not thinking as much as you would if you had to do it all on your own and struggle. So that’s effort. And so we can predict that using AI use would reduce effort. In our experiments, that’s exactly what we found. During the practice period where you had this AI tool, you used fewer keystrokes, you spent less time. So yeah, when you’ve got an assistant, you will work less, and that should diminish your skill. I think everyone is correct to worry that AI use is going to make them lazy and stupid because all things being equal, if you reduce your effort, you will learn less. You will improve less. However, I think what we’re forgetting about is a second box on this figure, and that is the quality of your learning environment. Let me give you an example. If you are Roger Federer and you are a young boy with lots of talent, imagine that you had a world-class coach, which he did. He did have a world-class coach who helped him realize his potential. Now, imagine you’re the same Roger Federer and you have a terrible tennis coach, somebody who can barely play tennis themselves, knows nothing about motivation. Now, that is going to degrade your learning environment. My point is that it’s a open question whether learning environment will be improved or diminished by AI use. But I think in our research, what we find is this. When AI can do something better than you can do, when AI can format a cover letter better than you can do, it increases the quality of the learning environment. And how does it do that? In the same way that a great coach does, which is to show you by example what you need to do. When Claude writes better than you, when ChatGPT comes up with an idea that you didn’t come up with, watch and learn. So much of human learning is by example. And therefore, I want to say that there is hope because even when we reduce effort, if we improve the learning environment enough, we can see improved skill over the long-term, which is what we found in our experiment. The great coach, John Wooden, who led UCLA to a record 10 NCAA basketball championships, boiled down learning to this little poem. Number one, explanation. Number two, demonstration. That’s what I’m talking about in terms of learning by example. Number three, imitation. So his players would see him do a move and they would copy it. And then repetition, repetition, repetition, repetition, repetition. I argue that in the age of AI, it is possible for your teams to get smarter and maybe even grittier if GPT or Claude is explaining what to do, demonstrating what to do, if we lean in and say, “We can watch and learn,” and then, of course, if we stay on the learning curve enough to become excellent at what we do. This is why I think it all comes back to having a steadfast goal, a top-level goal that you’re sticky about, but being agile and adaptive at the bottom, including embracing ways of using AI. In some, grit matters because it keeps you on a learning curve. And you will never be great unless you keep climbing some learning curve in life. Number two, young workers today are using AI to boost their productivity, but they’re ambivalent. They worry that it makes them lazy and stupid. And finally, when AI does something better than you, learn by example. And I argue, be willing to outsource to AI the goals at the very bottom of your goal hierarchy where, frankly, you’re not learning at all, you’re just completing some chore or task. ADI IGNATIUS: Lots to talk about, lots of questions coming in. I do want to ask one quick question of my own, which is, and I should remember this because I’ve heard you say this before, but you talked about grit, long-term perseverance, a need to finish what you start. How many of us have that? ANGELA DUCKWORTH: Well, Adi, I will say this. Like most of human- ADI IGNATIUS: Is that a rare quality or is that a common attribute? ANGELA DUCKWORTH: … qualities, it’s not either/or. It’s how much. So you can be very, very, very gritty. You can be just very gritty. You can be sort of gritty. You can be not very gritty. You can be extremely ungritty. So it is a continuum. I do think that when you look at the Michael Phelpses of the world, the Katie Ledeckys, or the titans of industry and finance, I mean, almost always they are outliers in grit among other things, by the way, because I don’t think grit is enough. It is necessary, it is not sufficient. And so wherever you are, you’re on the continuum, Adi. I am too. And what I will say is this, if there’s one singular insight that should give you hope, it is that wherever you are in the continuum, we find that grit changes. And in particular with age and with experience, on average, people get grittier. My argument is that if you understand what is in the head of a gritty person, if you understand goal hierarchies, for example, and the importance of a top-level goal and the importance of being flexible at the bottom of a goal hierarchy, you can catalyze. You can accelerate the development of your own grit. ADI IGNATIUS: You talked about the question of whether AI is going to dumb us down or weaken our skills and ability. And you talked about John Wooden, the coach example. The coach shows you what to do. You learn from that. But AI, it almost seems like the coach doesn’t just show you once how to shoot a layup. It does it for you for eternity. So here’s one of the questions that came in. This is from Begum Avdagic, product manager at Dewhurst UK. If grid is about sustained effort toward long-term goals, is offloading this cognitive work to AI undermining that muscle you’re trying to develop? ANGELA DUCKWORTH: I want to agree with this concern, which is that if you continuously offload all cognitive work to AI… I mean, when I say that the human brain and the human body are adaptive, I really mean it. And it goes in both directions. I mean, anybody who’s had their arm in a cast is just shocked to see how quickly it atrophies. So we are plastic. We can grow. We can grow smarter. We can grow dumber. We can grow more gritty. We can grow less gritty. So it’s not a guarantee that the gains are always going to be monotonic. So I think it’s a terrific concern. But let me give you the example of the graduate student who led that research. When AI debuted and changed everyone’s lives, he was one of the very first to realize that. He walked into the door of my office. He said, “I’m dropping everything and I’m going to study AI.” I didn’t even know what he was talking about. Then actually in the next few months, he got a little discouraged. He was like, “I spent my whole 20s learning how to program, and now I cannot program as well as GPT.” And those were early models by the way. So there was a stages of grief. It was like, “Oh, I just trained my whole life to do something and I cannot do it as well as this mindless bot.” Then what happened was two things. One is Ben learned to delegate the kind of tasks that really there wasn’t much of a learning curve. He just had to get them done. Really tedious tests, formatting tables, putting the numbers into a manuscript that we were going to publish and then editing it and making sure that it was in APA format. He delegates those tedious tests to AI. So he’s not getting better at them, but it doesn’t matter. He has freed up hours and hours of his day to do the kind of high-quality work at the top of the goalie hierarchy that he really wants to do. And as I said, he does learn from example. When he asks Claude or GPT to do some coding for him, which is what he does, because we’re, of course, all programming that way, he can see the code. And sometimes he’s like, “Oh, God, why didn’t I think of that?” So I think a lot of it boils down to how you choose to use AI. If you are going to cognitively offload everything and choose not to learn and improve, then you will become lazier and stupider. That’s absolutely true. But if you choose to free up time so you can do higher-level thinking and every time you use AI, if you ask yourself, “Could I learn something from this? Could I myself, as a human, get better?”, then I think the opposite will be true. ADI IGNATIUS: Laziness and stupidity is a choice. Okay, so here’s a question from Satoi, who is a graduate student at Harvard who says, “Hi, Angela. I’m a huge fan. Thank you for presenting. When you say watch and learn, how do you ensure that your team isn’t just watching and moving on, but actually taking the time for it?” ANGELA DUCKWORTH: I do think you need to have a mindset about this that some would argue is a maximizing mindset. So the great Nobel Laureate, Herb Simon, who is no longer alive, but he taught for years at Carnegie Mellon, and he is really a giant. I mean, a giant even among the Nobel Laureates. And he distinguished between maximizing and satisficing. And in a lot of life, you want to satisfice, which means good enough is good enough. You go out to lunch and the chicken salad sandwich is eh, but you’re not going to ruminate about it all day. It’s like, “It was good enough. We had lunch. What are we doing this afternoon?” And you can make the argument, David Epstein makes this argument in his latest book, Inside the Box, that that’s exactly what you should do for many things. But as somebody who has studied Olympians and somebody who’s studied three-star Michelin chefs, and as somebody who has studied really the world-changing CEOs, I will tell you that if you commit to excellence, there is a domain in your life where you say, “I am not a satisficer. I am a maximizer. Good is never good enough.” If you have this mindset, if you say, “As a psychologist, I want to become a better psychologist,” if as a manager, you want to become a better manager, as a strategist, I want to become a better strategist, then every time you’re interacting with AI, you’re asking yourself, “How is this going to improve me?” I’m delegating tedious tasks. I don’t have to do that anymore. I’ve got four hours to do something really hard and important. Great. Or I watched and I learned. So it’s not just what you’re given, it’s what you’re taking from this interaction with this new technology. ADI IGNATIUS: Yep. All right, here’s a question from someone identifying themselves as Dr. Indira, CEO and founder at EmpowerU. And the question is, it’s interesting, from an AI ethics and human-centric governance perspective, when younger workers express ambivalence about AI, it might be less about whether or not they have grit or whether they’re open to change, but more a rational response to the accountability gaps when you don’t know who is responsible when AI is wrong. So how should leaders address that kind of implicit structural dimension besides the motivational one? AI ambivalence may not just be, “Come on, you’re not changing with the times. You don’t have grit. Let’s get moving here,” but maybe a more rational wait-and-see approach to a technology that isn’t proven, that makes mistakes, has accountability gaps. So it’s saying you’re not getting with AI… It may not be just about grit – ANGELA DUCKWORTH: And by the way, Adi, I don’t think I ever said, “Get with the program. Be gritty.” By the way, that helped nobody ever. I have two daughters. I never once said, “Amanda, be gritty.” I never once said, “Lucy, be gritty.” I actually think that’s like… Bumper sticker psychology doesn’t work. I don’t think that’s the message of this talk. So the message of the talk is grit is about being devoted to a top-level goal and being flexible about how you get there. But I will say to this excellent question, if I interpret it correctly, I think most of human responses are rational. Why do I think that? It’s because people are not waking up in the morning and thinking, “I’m going to make a logical mistake.” Now, do people make mistakes? Absolutely. But almost always there is something that you’re responding to in a sensible way, even if it might be incomplete or myopic. So when people have this hesitation about AI, I think it is for good reason. I’ve hoped to have made that point that yes, absolutely AI can make you lazy and stupid. I also think it can make mistakes. So yes, hallucinations are still possible. And more than that, when you have this giant genie that does auto complete, it’s like playing hangman. It’s like C-A-T, C-A-N, more likely than C-A-X. So this thing that we don’t fully understand ourselves that’s magical in its abilities, but we also have a very different way of thinking. Human beings don’t think with auto complete. We should be hesitant. That’s a rational concern, not just because of lazy and stupid concerns, but also because we don’t fully understand how this genie works. So I think all those things are true, and yet I am among those who say, “If you don’t wake up every day and ask yourself, ‘How can my company use AI to improve,’ then you are an ostrich with your head in the ground.” The hesitance is itself a decision. The hesitation is itself an action. And so we don’t really have a choice. When Ben Lira walked through my door and said, “I’m dropping everything I’m doing and I’m working on AI,” I couldn’t believe it. And I though he might be wrong, but now in 2026, I think he was exactly right. ADI IGNATIUS: This is a question from Simon, who works on HR tech strategy and transformation at BHP. And he asks, he says, “Your concept of situational agency, designing environments rather than relying on willpower,” the question says makes intuitive sense at an individual level, but what does it look like when leaders try to apply it at scale across a big organization and where can that framework break down? ANGELA DUCKWORTH: I spent the first half of my life answering a question which is why are some people more successful? And I looked the first place you would look, which is you look at the person and you’re like, “What are their personal qualities?” And you notice that Michael Phelps is really gritty. You’re like, “Whoa, this kid didn’t miss a practice for 10 years.” And by the way, when Michael Phelps was training, he didn’t train five days a week. He didn’t train six days a week. He trained seven days a week. So you’re like, the answer to the question, what makes some people more successful than others, is the personal quality of grit. That was the first half of my career. The second half of my career, I’ve been trying to answer the same exact question. What makes some people more successful? But instead of looking inside the person for their personal qualities, I’ve been looking without. I’ve been looking outside them. Who coached Michael Phelps? Where did Michael Phelps train? What kind of team was he on? What culture was he in? And that’s what I mean by situational agency, your ability to change your environment in ways that bring out your best. Michael Phelps had a coach from when he was 11 to when he retired at 31. That coach is Bob Bowman, the best swim coach in history. If Bob Bowman were a country, he would rank pretty high in medals for swimming at the Olympics. He had the best coach in the world. Where did he grow up? He grew up in Baltimore, 10 minutes away from the premier aquatic youth center in the world. 10 minutes away. Two 50-meter pools, one inside, one outside, and world-class competition. How many of you can say, “Oh yeah, I also grew up there”? What kind of team was Michael Phelps on? Michael Phelps was on a team where people went to the Olympics all the time. They broke records all the time. And finally, what kind of culture was Michael in? Well, I’ll tell you, he had a culture at that team that Bob Bowman created, a culture of excellence, as Bob Bowman said, and he also had the world’s best mom. Debbie Phelps raised her three children in a culture of excellence. So when I talk about situational agency, I say, “Well, some of that’s luck, of course, what your situation is, but some of it you create.” Michael followed Bob Bowman when Bob changed locations. He followed him because he knew he had the best coach. He always navigated to be around the best teammates. He tried to not spend time with people who didn’t bring out his best. He always cared about the quality of his physical training facilities. So my last word to you, Adi, is that grit is important, but so is your situation. And if you want to be your best, you not only have to have passion and perseverance for a top-level goal, you also have to be deliberate about your physical situation, where you keep your phone, about your social situation, who you are working with on a team, who your mentors are. And of course, ultimately what every leader worries about, you have to be very intentional about culture. I don’t think so. ADI IGNATIUS: I wonder if Debbie Phelps told her kids, “Be gritty.” ANGELA DUCKWORTH: I don’t think so. ADI IGNATIUS: So we are out of time, but Angela thank you so much for your insights, thank you so much for being with us. That was fantastic. ANGELA DUCKWORTH: Thank you, Adi. Thank you, HBR. ADI IGNATIUS: That was Angela Duckworth, professor at the University of Pennsylvania and author of Grit, as well as the forthcoming book, Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best. If you found this episode helpful, share it and rate us in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, please consider heading to hbr.org/subscribe to get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Thanks to our team, senior producer Mary Dooe, and senior production editor Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Adi Ignatius.

item.title: inReach Messenger Plus: Photo & Voice Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 6.26
Garmin inReach Messenger Plus Review Updated August 2026 Jump to a section The inReach for phone-first users, with up to 600 hours of battery life against the Mini 3 Plus’s 350. Cumbersome to use without a phone. The first inReach with Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT) that gives you 1,600-character messages, voice notes, and photos. Performance was top-notch, even in dense Redwood canopy. But typing on the device with its small screen and minimal buttons is slow, so plan on using the Garmin Messenger app for almost everything. If you want a device that works well with or without an app, get the Mini 3 Plus Video Here’s a video I made using the Messenger Plus out on the trail so you can see how it works in real-world conditions. vs. Messenger Should you upgrade from the original inReach Messenger? Not unless you specifically need images or voice notes. | Feature | Messenger Plus | Messenger | |---|---|---| | Price | $499 | $299 | | Messaging System | Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT) | Short Burst Data (SBD) | | Voice Messages | Yes (via app) | No | | Photo Messages | Yes (via app) | No | | Message Length | Up to 1600 characters | Up to 160 characters | | App Compatibility | Messenger & Explore | Messenger only | | Battery Life | Up to 600 hours | Up to 672 hours | | Subscription Rates | Higher for image/voice | Standard | Features The Messenger Plus is built around Garmin’s switch from Iridium’s older Short Burst Data (SBD) protocol to Iridium Messaging Transport (IMT), which is faster and supports larger payloads. In practice, that enables: - Photo and voice messaging: Record a voice note or send a photo via satellite when paired to a phone. Garmin Response can receive both in an SOS. - 1,600-character messages: The old 160-character limit is gone. Longer messages go through in full when sent to a phone or another Plus device. - Tapbacks and emojis: Standard smartphone messaging tools, no message credit cost for tapbacks. - Garmin Explore compatibility: Unlike the original Messenger, the Plus works with Garmin Explore for offline maps, routes, and waypoints via phone. Speed - Messenger Plus was about 20-30% faster overall, but not dramatically so. - Both devices sent standard messages in under 2 minutes in most conditions. - Photo messages sometimes took 10 minutes or longer in dense forest. The 10+ minute figure was under heavy Redwood tree cover, which is a good stress test for satellite signal. Under normal conditions, open sky or light cover, Garmin specs and other testers put typical photo or voice send time closer to 1-2 minutes. If your trips are mostly above treeline or in open terrain, you’ll see much faster results than my worst-case numbers. Messaging - 1,600-character messages go through in full when sent to a phone or another Plus. Sent to a traditional inReach like a Mini 2 or GPSMAP 67i, they break into 160-character chunks, each counting as a separate message on the receiving end. - Voice messages are useful. Record in the app, it sends as an audio file. The limit is 30 seconds, short enough that some people are caught off guard. Voice notes can’t be sent to older inReach models. - Photos are compressed but clear enough for trail documentation and emergency use. One thing nobody mentions upfront: recipients need the Garmin Messenger app installed to receive photos and voice messages. Standard SMS contacts get text only. If your emergency contacts or family don’t have the app, they won’t receive anything beyond a text message, worth sorting out before you leave the trailhead. Emergency - SOS still routes through Garmin Response, which can now receive voice notes and photos from the Plus. - Being able to send an image of an injury or describe a situation by voice instead of typing is a real upgrade in a serious emergency. Navigation - Connecting to Garmin Explore unlocks offline maps, routes, and waypoints, but the app uses your phone’s GPS rather than the device’s. The Plus has onboard GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou, but no multi-band. - Trackback functionality had bugs at launch but has been addressed in firmware. - If navigation matters, this isn’t the device. Use the GPSMAP 67i or pair your phone with an inReach Mini 3. Battery The new Certus protocol can burn more battery depending on how you use it. Garmin offers two modes: - Performance mode maintains a near-constant satellite link for fast back-and-forth messaging. Battery drains fast, especially in heavy cover where the signal is intermittent. - Low power mode checks for messages roughly once an hour, similar to older inReach models. Battery life improves dramatically. Real-world battery was more variable than older inReach devices. Garmin specs performance mode at up to 110 hours with 10-minute tracking and no media, but that’s a light-use baseline. In heavy tree cover using performance mode with several images and messages sent, I was tracking around 22 hours. That’s a stress test, not typical use. In open sky on low power mode with 10-minute location tracking, the battery barely moved over a 5-hour hike. Default to low power mode unless you’re expecting active back-and-forth communication.

item.title: Garmin inReach SOS: How It Works & When to Use It
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.71
Garmin inReach SOS Guide Jump to a section The SOS button is the most important feature on a satellite communicator, and the one people understand the least. It’s not the same as calling 911. An inReach SOS routes to Garmin Response, a 24/7 center that coordinates with local rescue teams and messages with you the whole time. Here’s when to hit it and what to actually expect if you do. When to SOS - Unsure of a safe outcome? Hit it. The best advice I’ve heard, from an LA County search and rescue veteran: if you’re not sure you’ll be okay, press SOS. It’s two-way, so you can describe the situation, lost, stranded, chest pain, and Garmin Response helps you figure out what to do. - Not just for the backcountry. Garmin’s own SOS data is full of vehicle use: cars, boats, motorcycles. Carry it when you drive out of cell range, because a flat or a breakdown can just mean a tow, not a helicopter. - Medical issues and injuries are the top reasons people hit it. A pre-existing condition doesn’t disqualify you. If something feels wrong, ask. - More than half of SOS calls are for someone else. Like calling 911 as a Good Samaritan, hitting SOS for another person doesn’t make you liable. Just know that rescue insurance only covers you, not them. - Don’t abuse it. Being tired or having a sore stomach isn’t an emergency. Use common sense, same as you would with 911. Hitting the Button - There’s a countdown. Once you trigger it, the device counts down before the message goes out, and you can cancel during that window. - Sent one by mistake? Cancel it, don’t power off. Cancel the SOS on the device and reply to Garmin Response so they know you’re okay. Powering off leaves them assuming the worst, and a search may start anyway. - False alarms don’t cost you. Garmin doesn’t charge for an accidental activation you cancel. Cancelling isn’t an embarrassment, it’s the system working. - SOS can stay active on a suspended plan. On compatible devices you keep a working SOS button even with messaging suspended. Details on the subscription page. What Happens When You Hit SOS - A helicopter is not the default. Garmin’s data shows most rescues aren’t helicopters. They’re usually local volunteers organized by a sheriff’s department or park service. - It takes hours to mobilize. Even a helicopter rescue usually takes several hours. Be ready to wait, and carry enough to spend the night: an emergency bivy, extra layers, and food. - Rescue comes in many forms. It might be self-evacuation with guidance, a ground team, a cliff extraction, or just a ranger walking you down. I’ve seen that on Mount Whitney for altitude sickness. About 10% of people handle it themselves. - You stay in contact the whole time. Unlike a one-way PLB, Garmin Response keeps messaging you updates until help arrives. Rescue Costs Triggering SOS is included in every inReach plan, so there’s no charge to hit the button. The rescue itself is a separate question. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can run well over $20,000. That’s what rescue insurance is for, and I break down the options on that page.

item.title: South Kaibab Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.64
South Kaibab Trail Updated July 2026 Jump to a section Grand Canyon views hit you immediately on South Kaibab, a ridge trail with zero water or shade. Three natural turnaround points at 1.8, 3, or 6 miles let you dial in your distance, but most day hikers stop at Skeleton Point where the exposure gets serious. - Distance - 1.8–6 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 600–2200 ft - Time - 1–5 hrs Video Options - You can choose how far you want to hike down the South Kaibab Trail. Simply turn around and hike back up from the destination that you’re hiking to. - Cedar Ridge is the farthest the National Park Service recommends going on a summer day hike. - Similarly, they also don’t recommend continuing past Skeleton Point as a day hike outside of summer without consulting with a park ranger. Info Kaibab is a word of Southern Paiute origin meaning “mountain lying down,” aka inverted mountain. Difficulty Overall the South Kaibab Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. - When people get into trouble on the South Kaibab Trail, it’s usually because of the heat. The trail is totally exposed with no shade, so in hot weather it can be brutal. Even in the shade, summer temperatures often exceed 100F (38C). Check the weather and park alerts regarding the heat. - The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. - Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. - Outside of the trailhead and Colorado River, there is no water anywhere on the South Kaibab Trail. You have to carry all the water you need, and in summer that can mean several liters per person. - The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. But people have also died after getting too close to the edge (taking pictures). Be conservative. - Mules also use the trail, so be ready to step aside in safe areas when they pass. Trailhead The road to the South Kaibab Trailhead (Yaki Point Road) is closed to vehicles. Here’s what I would recommend. - Take the free Orange shuttle bus from the Visitor Center. This is by far the easiest way to get back and forth to the trail. If you want to get an early start, take the Hiker’s Express Shuttle, which is set up for long distance hikers but can be used by anyone. Getting an early start is a smart way to beat the crowds and see the sunrise in the canyon. - You can also walk from the Visitor Center along the wide and easy Rim Trail. It’s about 2.2 miles and takes most folks around 40-60 minutes. - There’s a very small parking lot along Desert View Drive, not intended for hikers but rather as a turn-off for drivers. From here you can walk about 0.5 miles to the Rim Trail and then to the South Kaibab trailhead. Trailhead Address: South Kaibab Trailhead, Grand Canyon Village, AZ 86023 Fees: Park Entrance Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) Gear - As I mentioned earlier, you need to bring your water with you. To Ooh Ahh Point, 1L is fine. To Cedar Ridge or Skeleton Point, bring 2L or 3L when it’s hot. Better to have more water than you need. Bring a backpack to carry it along with sun protection. - The hiking community has generally moved from hiking boots to trail runners. Overall you want your feet to be comfortable, especially if you’re not used to hiking this far. If you don’t have trail runners, wear sneakers. - Some hikers like trekking poles, and they can be helpful for stability, knee protection (on the downhill), and climbing on the way back out. - Don’t count on cellular service. If you need to call for help, having a satellite-enabled phone or satellite communicator can help. The trail is busy, so even if you don’t have satellite communications, you’re likely to see someone who might. - It can help to have a snack and/or electrolyte drink for the way back up if you’re doing one of the longer options. Maps Directions Trailhead to Ooh Ahh Point Info The South Kaibab Trail was built by engineers in 1924-25 to create a smooth and direct route down to the river. It has been described as “a trail in a hurry to get to the river.” Info At the bottom of the canyon, the layers date back 1.84 BILLION years! To put that in perspective, the Earth is 4.543 billion years old. Info If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Ooh Ahh Point to Cedar Ridge Info While Cedar Ridge seems open and a great place to camp, no camping is allowed along the South Kaibab Trail. If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Cedar Ridge to Skeleton Point Info The South Kaibab Trail is part of the Arizona Trail (AZT), which stretches about 800 miles from Mexico to Utah.

item.title: Bright Angel Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.58
Start near Bright Angel Lodge with water stations, multiple turnaround points, and the gentlest descent into the Grand Canyon. The 4,000-foot climb out will still humble you. Distance 3–12 mi Difficulty Hard Total Climbing 1100–3060 ft Time 2–8 hrs Who It's ForReasonably fit hikers. Well-maintained trail, clear signs, water stations make it the most forgiving canyon hike. Biggest RiskHeat and overexertion, especially on uphill return. Winter snow/ice on upper sections, mornings. When to GoYear-round. Start at sunrise in summer. Winter, check for ice near rim. You can choose how far you want to hike down the Bright Angel Trail. Simply turn around and hike back up from the destination that you’re hiking to. The National Park Service doesn’t recommend continuing below Havasupai Gardens as a day hike for most hikers. Warning When you’re figuring out which option is right for you, know that 2,640 feet of climbing is 0.5 miles straight uphill and fairly tough for most folks. It’s not just the distance. Difficulty Overall the Bright Angel Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. As you descend 1000 feet, the temperature will rise around 3.5°F to 5.5°F. So if you descend to Havasupai Gardens, the temperature could be somewhere around 18.5°F hotter than where you started. And the temperature will continue to rise until mid-afternoon. There are some shaded parts of the trail but not much, it can get very hot. You need to check park alerts and weather for the heat and plan accordingly. Leaving at sunrise is a great way to beat the heat and the crowds at the same time. The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. An advantage of the Bright Angel Trail is that it follows the water pipeline. You should still carry water with you, and you can refill along the way. Check the park page before you go, the water is sometimes turned off in places. The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. Info Want to camp on the Bright Angel Trail? You can book a tent site at Havasupai Garden on Recreation.gov (Backcountry Permit > Classic GC Hike South Rim > Havasupai Gardens Campground). Fees: Park Entrance Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) The closest parking is in the lot right next to the trailhead, which is next to the Bright Angel Lodge. I’ve had success here or on the street nearby when arriving early. The biggest lot nearby is Parking Lot D by the Backcountry Information Center. It’s a 5-10 minute walk to the trailhead from here and there are usually spots open. Alternatively you can take free shuttles from a bigger parking area like the Visitor Center to the stop for Bright Angel Lodge. Gear Even though there’s water on the trail, bring some with you, you’ll need it. Bring a backpack to carry it along with sun protection. The hiking community has generally moved from hiking boots to trail runners. Overall you want your feet to be comfortable, especially if you’re not used to hiking this far. If you don’t have trail runners, wear sneakers. Some hikers like trekking poles, and they can be helpful for stability, knee protection (on the downhill), and climbing on the way back out. Don’t count on cellular service. If you need to call for help, having a satellite-enabled phone or satellite communicator can help. The trail is busy, so even if you don’t have satellite communications, you’re likely to see someone who might. Bring a snack and/or electrolyte drink for the way back up. Tip See all the gear I use on hikes like this on my gear page. Did you know that the Bright Angel Trail used to be private and cost $1 (about $40 today) to hike? The path was used by Havasupai for hundreds of years but in the 1890s a settler claimed this land and started charging visitors to hike. Even after the Grand Canyon became a park in 1919 it was still private. The National Park Service was able to end private control by 1927. Hiking to 1.5 Mile Resthouse Info Pictographs = painted, Petroglyphs = carved Info These rest houses were built in 1935-1936 by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). Hiking to 3 Mile Resthouse Hiking to Havasupai Garden Info Havasupai Gardens was formerly known as “Indian Garden” and you may see some references to that on maps or signs. Info Theodore Roosevelt (who rode down the Bright Angel Trail on a horse) ordered the Havasupai who lived here to leave in 1901 in order to make way for the park. Some left and some stayed, but in 1928 the Parks Service forced the last Havasupai out of the Bright Angel area and onto a 518-acre reservation in Havasu Canyon. Info The fertile land at Havasupai Garden (around Garden Creek) has been cultivated since 300AD. Western tourists starting arriving in the 1890s and as you know, the last natives were moved out of here in 1928. Today there is a ranger station, toilets, picnic areas, a campground, and water. Info Havasupai means “people of the blue-green waters,” referring to the color of the Colorado River, which runs through the Grand Canyon. In the early 1900s they worked as laborers here and created much of what you see at Grand Canyon National Park. Hiking to Plateau Point Hiking Back To the South Rim The downhill is over, the hard part is yet to come. Unless you’re going to float down the river, you’ll have to walk back up to leave the inside of the Canyon.

item.title: ZOLEO Review: Still Worth It?
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.48
ZOLEO Review Updated August 2026 Jump to a section Inexpensive hardware, same Iridium network as Garmin, and the most seamless satellite messaging I’ve tested. If your phone is already how you navigate, this is worth a serious look. I’ve used the ZOLEO over the years on backcountry trips. At $149 upfront, the hardware is less expensive than any comparable inReach, and depending on your messaging volume the monthly cost can land lower too. It runs on the same Iridium network as Garmin. The Wi-Fi/cellular/satellite switching is the best implementation I’ve tested: one app, automatic handoff, no thinking required. The trade-offs are zero navigation and total phone dependence for anything beyond check-ins and SOS. The only reason to spend more on a Garmin inReach is if you want standalone navigation or you’re already deep in the Garmin ecosystem. For phone-first hikers, ZOLEO is the right call. Video Features The ZOLEO is a satellite messenger designed to work with your smartphone. Unlike Garmin’s inReach devices, there’s no screen or full interface on the unit itself. You pair it with the ZOLEO app via Bluetooth, and that’s where you handle messaging, weather forecasts, and settings. Without your phone, the ZOLEO still works for the essentials. Physical buttons handle SOS, check-in, and location sharing. LED indicators tell you what’s happening: green means it worked, red means it didn’t. What it does: - Two-way messaging (through the app) via satellite, Wi-Fi, or cell, whichever is available - Unlimited check-in messages with “I’m OK” and a map link to your GPS location - Breadcrumb trail location sharing with your contacts (optional $6/month add-on) - Weather reports for your current or custom locations - SOS with 24/7 emergency response coordination through GlobalRescue - Medical Assist messaging with health professionals (included on all plans) The biggest weakness is clear: you’re depending on your phone for the advanced functionality. If your phone dies, breaks, or loses Bluetooth, you’re limited to one-way SOS and check-ins. Advantages - Seamless messaging: ZOLEO gives you a real phone number and email address. You message with the same app whether you’re on Wi-Fi, cellular, or satellite, and it switches automatically. Garmin units don’t have their own number. - $4/month suspend: Garmin now offers 12 months of free suspension with SOS still active during that window. ZOLEO’s $4/month suspend doesn’t get you SOS you don’t already have, but it keeps your phone number and email live while paused, which Garmin’s suspension doesn’t. Garmin’s lowest active plan is $7.99/month for SOS only. - Medical Assist included: Contact a medical professional for advice before triggering SOS. Smart middle ground when something feels off but isn’t a clear emergency. - Rescue insurance available: Optional rescue insurance for around $40 covers the cost of an actual rescue. You can also sign up for the Overwatch & Rescue subscription, which is like AAA for the backcountry. - Proven durability: I’ve used mine in dust, rain, snow, and it’s taken some hits. It’s not flashy, but it works. Performance Across every trip I’ve used it on, messaging has been seamless and works exactly as advertised: you move between Wi-Fi, cell, and satellite without thinking about it. It just sends. The GPS does take longer to lock than my Garmin devices, which means check-ins sometimes take a minute or two longer to go out. I’ve had the occasional failed send too, but that’s become less common over time. Nothing that’s made me want to stop using it, and nothing that’s left me stranded. Subscriptions Both brands charge a $39.99 activation fee on first sign-up. After that, the monthly costs diverge. ZOLEO Plans | Plan | Monthly | Satellite Messages | Overage | Tracking | |---|---|---|---|---| | Basic | $20 | 75 | $0.50/msg | +$6/mo | | In Touch | $35 | 300 | $0.50/msg | +$6/mo | | Unlimited | $50 | Unlimited | Free | +$6/mo | All ZOLEO plans include unlimited check-ins, unlimited SOS, and Medical Assist. Suspend for $4/month; your phone number and email address stay active while suspended. Garmin inReach Plans | Plan | Monthly | Satellite Messages | Tracking | |---|---|---|---| | Enabled | $7.99 | Pay-per-use ($0.50/msg) | $0.10/point | | Essential | $14.95 | 50 | $0.10/point | | Standard | $29.99 | 150 | Unlimited (10 min) | | Premium | $49.99 | Unlimited | Unlimited (2 min) | All Garmin plans include unlimited SOS. Suspend free for up to 12 months, and SOS stays active during suspension, though messaging requires an active plan. No reactivation fee. The key difference: ZOLEO’s cheapest full-messaging plan ($20) gets you 75 messages and unlimited check-ins. Garmin’s Enabled plan ($7.99) gives you SOS and pay-per-use everything else. If you send more than a handful of messages per trip, ZOLEO’s $20 Basic is a better value than Garmin’s Enabled tier. If you primarily need SOS and check-ins with occasional messaging, Garmin’s Enabled plan is hard to beat at $7.99. Battery Advertised at 200+ hours with message checks every 12 minutes. Real-world numbers from my testing: - 12-minute message checks + 12-minute location shares: 88 hours - 12-minute message checks + 1-hour location shares: 140 hours - 12-minute message checks only: 190 hours Those numbers hold up on backpacking trips and thru-hikes. Increase check intervals and turn off location sharing to extend further. vs. inReach The inReach Messenger is the closest Garmin competitor. Both use Iridium, both rely on your smartphone for messaging, both include SOS. The differences come down to navigation, battery, and ecosystem. | Feature | ZOLEO | inReach Messenger | |---|---|---| | Price | $149 | $299 | | Coverage | Iridium global | Iridium global | | App Experience | Comparable | Comparable | | Location Sharing | Good | Better | | GPS Chipset | GPS/GLONASS | GPS/Galileo/QZSS/BeiDou | | Navigation | None | Very limited | | Battery Life | 200+ hours | 672 hours | | Connector | Micro USB | USB-C | | Weight | 150g (5.3 oz) | 114g (4.0 oz) | | Suspend | $4/month | 12 months free | | Activation Fee | $39.99 | $39.99 | The inReach Messenger wins on battery life (672 vs 200+ hours), weight (36g lighter), USB-C, multi-GNSS, and free 12-month suspension. The ZOLEO wins on device price ($150 cheaper), having a real phone number, and $4/month suspend that keeps your number and email active. If you’re in the Garmin ecosystem with watches and handhelds, the Messenger makes more sense. If you want lower hardware cost and seamless messaging on Iridium, ZOLEO is the right call.

item.title: Garmin inReach Subscription Cost: Which Plan Is Cheapest
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.47
Garmin inReach Subscription Cost Jump to a section A Garmin inReach subscription is required to use your device, and there’s a lot of variation in what you’ll pay. There are even inReach plans that Garmin doesn’t sell. Here’s how to figure out the best plan for you. | Plan | Best For | Price | |---|---|---| | Enabled | Pay only for what you use | $7.99/mo | | Standard | Sharing your live position with family on every hike | $29.99/mo | | ProteGear | Power users who want maximum flexibility | Pay per day | | Suspended | The cheapest way to keep 24/7 SOS (compatible devices) | ~$8/yr | Info I’ve paid for my own inReach device and subscription since 2014, when I got my first one. I buy all my own gear and don’t take sponsorships, so I’m free to use and recommend what works best. What You Get A Garmin inReach subscription is a monthly service plan, just like a cell phone plan. Two things have to be in place to get connected: an active subscription (these plans) and an inReach device to run it on. No plan means no SOS or messaging, even if you own the hardware. Here’s what a subscription unlocks: - Emergency SOS to the 24/7 Garmin Response center, who coordinate (but don’t perform) the rescue. Included on every plan, and still works when suspended on compatible devices - Two-way text messaging using satellite when you’re beyond cell range - Location tracking that shares a breadcrumb trail over satellite that others can follow on a map - Weather forecasts with hourly and multi-day outlooks, including a marine option - Photo and voice messages over satellite on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus and Mini 3 Plus - Check-in messages, three preset “I’m OK” type messages you can send for less than a normal message Pricing Levels Pricing on each plan is purely based on how much you use it. The more expensive the plan, the more usage you essentially prepay for. | Plan | Price/mo | Annual | Texts/Weather | Photo/Voice | Live Tracking | Check-ins | Text Overage | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Enabled | $7.99 | $95.88 | $0.50 ea | $1.00 ea | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | $0.10 ea | $0.50/msg | | Essential | $14.99 | $179.88 | 50 | 25 | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Standard | $29.99 | $359.88 | 150 | 50 | Unlimited (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Premium | $49.99 | $599.88 | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited (2 min+) | Unlimited | N/A | - There’s a one-time $39.99 activation fee on all plans, charged on every device, including inReach smartwatches like the Fenix 8 Pro. - A weather forecast counts as one satellite text message. - Incoming messages count too, including replies to your check-ins. - Emoji reactions (tapbacks) to messages in the Garmin Messenger app are billed the same as check-ins: free/unlimited on Essential, Standard, and Premium, and $0.10 each on Enabled. - Messages sent over Wi-Fi or cell through the Garmin Messenger app don’t count against your plan. Only satellite messages do. - Live tracking points always go out over satellite, so they’re always charged, even if your phone has signal. - A group message counts as a single message, but each reply costs a message. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus, GPSMAP H1i Plus, and Mini 3 Plus. - You can switch between plans at any time for free. You can also keep more than one device active on a single account (a new option since the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro), but each one needs its own activation fee and subscription. - Every plan includes Emergency SOS messaging through Garmin Response. - The plan prices are identical whether you carry a Mini 2, Mini 3, Messenger, or a GPSMAP. Garmin charges for the plan, not the device, so the “Garmin inReach Mini 2 subscription cost” is the same as the Mini 3 or Messenger. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices, so on an older unit like the Mini 2 those rows simply don’t apply. - Smartwatches with inReach (like the Fenix 8 Pro) add unlimited LTE messaging and calling when you have cell service. Cost Calculator Enter your estimated monthly usage and how many months a year you use the device, and this shows the monthly and annual cost for each plan. Click “Edit Charges” to adjust pricing for your local currency or region. Edit Charges Simply change the numbers here based on your currency. Overages | Plan | Monthly | Annual | |---|---|---| | Enabled | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Essential | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Standard | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Premium | $0.00 | $0.00 | Annual is your monthly cost times the months you use it, assuming you suspend for $0 the rest of the year. Year one adds a one-time $39.99 activation fee on every plan. - Most people: Enabled, about $146 a year. Full SOS, and you only pay for the tracking and messages you actually use. - Track every hike? Standard. Unlimited tracking beats Enabled once you pass about 36 tracking hours a month. - Essential rarely wins. It only makes sense for steady messaging with almost no tracking. Any real tracking, around 25 hours a month, pushes you to Standard. - Premium is niche. It’s only worth it above about 190 messages a month, or if you need 2-minute tracking, like guiding a team or sailing. - Seasonal user? Suspend. Keep SOS on a compatible device for about $8 a year instead of paying all year. Suspending You can suspend your plan for $0 for up to 12 consecutive months, with no reactivation fee. This is the move for seasonal users, and it beats canceling, which wipes your data and charges a fresh $39.99 activation fee to come back. The big deal is SOS. On compatible devices, Emergency SOS keeps working while your plan is suspended, even though messaging, tracking, and weather are off. That means you can carry a working SOS beacon in the off-season for almost nothing. To qualify, it has to be a compatible device, on the latest firmware, and previously on an active plan before you suspend. Not every device supports it, and the list keeps growing, so check Garmin’s current compatible-device list before you count on it. Older units like the original Mini and Explorer don’t qualify. After 12 consecutive months suspended, Garmin automatically moves the device onto the Enabled plan ($7.99/mo) to keep SOS alive. So the real cost of free suspended SOS is one paid month every 13: twelve months free, then the single auto-Enabled month before you suspend again. Call it about $8 a year. Third Party Plans A few partners resell the same Iridium connection with different pricing. ProteGear is the one worth knowing, and its whole angle is pay-per-day instead of per-month. - Pay-per-day. A €49 yearly base, then only the days you’re active, from about €1.50/day (safety) to €6/day (expedition). Flip it on and off yourself for free. - Same safety net. SOS still routes to Garmin Response, and you keep the Garmin Explore account and apps. - Extras Garmin dropped or lacks. Editable preset messages, a dedicated two-way email address, tracking down to 30 seconds, better weather reports, and Wikipedia or Google News over satellite. - The catches. The dashboard and setup are power-user territory and can be confusing, but human support is excellent and responsive. If you’re in Australia or New Zealand, TrackMeNZ is another third party option. inReach Rentals If you only go off-grid occasionally, renting can beat buying a device and paying for a plan. Outfitters will mail you a unit for your trip, usually around $10 to $15 per day with a few-day minimum. The typical flow: - Order online and choose a data plan and insurance. - The device ships to your home or a pickup location. - You get setup instructions by email. - Use it, then mail it back. I don’t have any specific company I recommend. Google “Garmin inReach rentals” and compare options. inReach Professional Garmin’s Professional plans are built for teams, organizations, and families that want one account across multiple devices. - Central management. Run multiple devices under one login, assign them to users, and monitor everyone from a single dashboard. - Best for. Guides, SAR teams, land managers, and anyone coordinating a group in the field. - Pricing. Tiered by how much messaging and tracking your team needs, billed monthly. See Garmin’s Professional plans for current rates. - Off-season. You can suspend Pro devices and still keep SOS on compatible units, so a fleet doesn’t lose emergency coverage when it’s stood down. Rescue Costs Your subscription pays for the SOS service, not the rescue itself. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can cost thousands, which is what rescue insurance covers.

item.title: Mount Perry Hike from Dante's Ridge Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.44
Mount Perry Hike from Dante's Ridge (Death Valley) Updated July 2026 Jump to a section Follow Dante’s Ridge 9 miles across the widest panorama in Death Valley, walking the spine of the Black Mountains 5,000 feet above Badwater Basin with views stretching to the Sierra Nevada. Almost nobody else attempts this point-to-point hike, stick to cooler months. Distance 9 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 2100 ft Time 4–5 hrs Who It's ForModerate hikers, 9 miles, 1,400 ft gain from 5,475 ft. Ridge walk, unmarked sections need navigation skills. Biggest RiskUnmarked route requires navigation. Significant wind exposure on ridge. Do not hike summer. When to GoOctober through May. Summer temperatures extreme even at elevation. This is a rugged and fairly remote hike. Don’t expect to see others and prepare for the conditions, which are often windy and exposed. Even though it’s cooler at this altitude than lower in Badwater Basin, it can still get extremely hot here. In the winter it can be freezing but don’t expect snow. In the summer, temperatures can be deadly. Checking the weather and conditions before you do this hike is critical. Bring at least 3L of water when it’s warm out. The trail is rocky and overall in good condition. Trail runners are a good choice for footwear. There is intermittent cellular service along the route but nothing dependable. If you have a satellite messenger, I’d bring it. Tip See all the gear I use on hikes like this on my gear page. Badwater Basin is the lowest point in North America at -282 feet. During the last Ice Age there was a massive lake there called Lake Manly. The water dried up about 10,000 years ago but occasionally heavy rains will create mini-lakes in the basin.

item.title: Hermit Trail to Santa Maria Spring Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.38
Grand Canyon National Park Hermit Trail to Santa Maria Spring Updated July 2026
Jump to a section
Follow the original 1911 sandstone-paved route down to a remote canyon shelter with views into Hermit Canyon. At 4.5 miles with shuttle access, you’ll have the trail nearly to yourself, making this one of the quietest ways into the Grand Canyon.
- Distance - 4.5 mi
- Difficulty - Hard
- Total Climbing - 1700 ft
- Time - 3–4 hrs Who It's For Hikers fit for steep sustained descents, prepared for the challenging climb out. Not technical but demanding. Biggest Risk Heat and overexertion on the return climb. Winter brings snow and ice hazards. When to Go Spring and fall ideal. Summer dangerously hot. Winter requires snow/ice preparation.
Video
Trailhead
Gear
This is a backcountry hike and you should prepare accordingly. - The Grand Canyon is a place of extremes. Prepare accordingly by checking the weather. In the winter, the trail can be covered in snow and ice. You’ll need micro-spikes and poles. - In the summer, temperatures can be deadly. If it’s hot out, skip the hike or leave before sunrise when temperatures are cooler. - When it’s hot, I bring 2L of water. Other times 1L is okay. - If you want to refill at Santa Maria Spring, you must treat the water with a filter. Trekking poles are helpful on the steep slopes. The trails are well-groomed and you can use trail runners. Don’t expect cellular coverage; bring a satellite communicator.

item.title: Do I Need SAR Insurance? Rescue Cost Coverage
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.35
Do I Need SAR Insurance? Jump to a section Your satellite communicator can call for a rescue, but it doesn’t pay for one. Most rescues are free, but that’s not always the case. Tip Quick pick: Overwatch x Rescue is what I use. It works on just about any device, including inReach and satellite-enabled phones. Rescue Costs Once you’ve asked for an evacuation, the rescue team will evaluate the situation and determine the best response. It could mean a ground team comes in and walks you out in a bucket, it could involve you self-evacuating to a meeting point, or could involve a helicopter rescue. If it does involve an aircraft, there can be a cost. The important thing to remember is that you don’t choose the response. - The rescue itself is usually free. Almost all search and rescue in the US is done by volunteers led by a sheriff or park team. If they have aircraft available, they can use it for the rescue and you aren’t charged. Some states will charge you for a rescue if you are negligent. - You pay for private services. The response may involve a private helicopter evacuation. It depends on the circumstances. Maybe a government helicopter is not available. Maybe your situation is so dire that you need a specialized air ambulance to take you directly to a specialized ER center. The average private air evacuation runs about $28,000, and you don’t get a say in whether one is used. - The hospital is separate. Once evacuated and admitted to care, your regular health insurance takes over. Rescue coverage gets you out of the backcountry, not the care that follows. Info Are you negligent? The test is the “reasonable person standard”: what a reasonable person would have done in your situation, which scales with your experience. Running a stop sign and causing a crash is negligent because a reasonable person stops. Hiking onto a closed trail or a route far beyond your ability can be treated the same way. Payment Options Knowing that a rescue could cost you, here are the options. - Health Insurance generally won’t cover an evacuation cost but it’s worth checking before you spend any extra money. - Local Cards are available for some areas. They support local SAR teams and cover any rescue costs. Two popular ones are New Hampshire’s Hike Safe card and Colorado’s CORSAR card. - Bundled Insurance with your device is usually an option for devices like ZOLEO, SPOT, and inReach. For inReach, Garmin sells SAR insurance plans from $39.95 to $999.95 a year depending on your needs. It’s insurance and you have to go through the claims process. - Overwatch x Rescue is like AAA for SAR, you pay one annual fee and that’s it. You can call them to coordinate a rescue or use Garmin Response, and unlike insurance, they simply cover the cost of rescue without a cumbersome claims process. - Other Options A simple Google search for SAR insurance will bring up lots of options, but I think for most users, the previously mentioned options make the most sense. Overwatch x Rescue This is the one I carry. I can put it on all my devices, their response center is the best I’ve come across, and it covers exactly what I need without a pile of fine print. Here’s what you get: - $79.99 a year, and it’s not insurance. It’s a fully funded service, so they pay the providers directly. No claim to file, no deductible, no reimbursement to chase. - Two fully funded responses a year, up to 10 days of assistance each. More than enough for most people. - Works on any satellite device, across more than one. A Garmin inReach, an iPhone or Android with satellite SOS, or a ZOLEO or SPOT, and you can cover several devices under one plan. - Risky sports are included. Mountaineering, rock climbing, skiing, and other hazardous summer and winter sports are covered for search and rescue and medical evacuation, with no surcharge. - It covers the whole way out. Search and rescue to the nearest hospital or safe harbor, plus medically necessary air transport to the nearest appropriate hospital. Your health insurance takes over from there. - International adds a lot. During foreign travel it also covers natural disasters, civil unrest, terrorism, wrongful detention, medical repatriation to a hospital back home, and flying a family member out if you’re hospitalized. Overwatch vs. Garmin | Feature | Overwatch x Rescue | Garmin Plan | |---|---|---| | Price | $79.99 | $39.95 | | Search & Rescue | ✓ | ✓ | | Medical Transport to Hospital | ✓ | ✗ | | Risky Activities Like Mountaineering | ✓ | $299.95 | | Above 5000m | ✓ | $999.95 | | No Monetary Limit per Response | ✓ | ✗ | | Family/Friend Hospital Visitation | ✓ | ✗ | | Home Hospital Repatriation | ✓ | ✗ | | Arctic & Antarctic | ✗ | ✓ | | Caving / Underground | ✗ | ✓ | | Intoxication, Self-Harm, War | ✗ | ✗ | | Can Purchase | Worldwide | US & Canada Only | | Claim | Pays Directly | You Pay & File Claim |

item.title: Guadalupe Peak Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.30
Guadalupe Peak Hike Updated August 2026 Jump to a section Guadalupe Peak punches 8,751 feet straight up from the Chihuahuan Desert on a rocky ridge of ancient Permian reef. This 8.4-mile climb gains 3,000 feet with relentless summit wind, but the payoff is Texas’s highest point and views that stretch into New Mexico and Mexico itself. - Distance - 8.4 mi - Difficulty - Hard - Total Climbing - 3000 ft - Time - 4–8 hrs Video Trailhead Guadalupe Peak is remote. - There is no gas station between El Paso and the park, or Carlsbad and the park. - Bring all the food you need with you. - You can refill with water at the Visitor Center or at the campground by the trailhead. - Guadalupe Mountains National Park is situated right on the edge of two time zones (Mountain and Central Standard Time), and the time on your phone could be incorrect. - If you’re wondering where to stay to visit here, there are hotels in El Paso and Carlsbad, or stay at a campground in the park bookable on Recreation.gov. Fees: $10 Day Use (or use your America the Beautiful pass) You can pay the entrance fee at the Visitor Center or with credit card machines at the trailheads. Trailhead Address: Pine Springs Trailhead, Salt Flat, TX 79847 Parking can be a big challenge for this hike. The main lot has about 44 spaces, but they can fill up quickly. Your best bet is to arrive at sunrise for the hike and you’re generally assured to get a spot. As the morning progresses it can get tougher and tougher, and often after 730am the parking lot can be full. If the lot is full, you’ll have to park at the Visitor Center (also not a big lot) and walk up from there. I’d say if you’re going to come all the way here to do the hike, get here around sunrise. Safety When to Hike | Season | Conditions | |---|---| | March-May | Usually good; can snow into April | | June-August | Very hot with afternoon thunderstorms | | September-November | Best time; fewer crowds | | December-February | Deadly snow, ice, and wind chills possible | - The main thing to watch out for is the weather. Conditions at 8,751 feet can be very different from those at the trailhead, so check the mountain forecast as well as the trailhead forecast before you go. I’ve heard that sometimes when the weather is extreme the rangers will turn hikers back before the summit. If the weather is questionable, call the Visitor Center. - Rattlesnakes live here and are most active in warmer months. If you see one sunning on the trail, give it space and wait for it to move off. They’re not aggressive unless provoked. If you’re putting your hands on rocks, look first, snakes often shelter in crevices. - If you have a medical condition affected by exertion or altitude, take it slow. The hike gains about 3,000 feet starting at roughly a mile above sea level, and it can be strenuous if you’re not used to big climbs. - Afternoon thunderstorms are frequent in summer, and lightning is a serious risk on the exposed upper slopes and summit. If the weather turns bad, turn around. - Watch your footing on the way back down. The trail is rocky and it can be easy to roll an ankle. Gear - The summit has its own weather. Pack an extra layer and shell. Winds can hit 50-80 mph up there. - Trekking poles are helpful when pacing uphill and when descending. - Trail runners work great on the Guadalupe Peak Trail. - Bring at least 3L of water, more if it’s hot out. There are no springs or water sources along the hike. You can fill up at the campground by the trailhead or at the Visitor Center. I bring my full water with me before leaving for the park just in case those water sources are not in service. - Snacks like trail mix and protein bars are a good bet. - Most of the trail is exposed, so bring sun protection. - This is a proper backcountry hike, so make sure you have the essentials to stay overnight if you need to. That includes a headlamp in case you get caught out after dark on the descent. - Most of the hike has okay cell phone coverage so you can call 911, but I bring a satellite SOS device just in case. Camping There’s a small backcountry campground about a mile below the summit, accessible only by hiking up the Guadalupe Peak Trail. It has a few tent pads and no water, so you’ll need to carry everything you need, including extra water for the night and descent. Camping here gives you a head start for sunrise or sunset at the summit, but be prepared for strong winds and cold temperatures, even in warmer months. Permits are required and available at the Pine Springs Visitor Center or on Recreation.gov in advance. Info After the first mile or so of climbing, it enters the Guadalupe Mountains Wilderness, and from there all human waste and toilet paper must be carried out. Bring a WAG Bag in case you have to “take care of business.” Maps Elevation Profile Directions Mile 0 - 1.5: The Big Effort The first 1.5 miles is the hardest part for many hikers. It’s steep, rocky, and doesn’t offer many spots to catch your breath. Info The El Capitan Trail goes to a viewpoint below it. There is no official trail to the top of El Capitan. Mile 1.5-3.3: The Breather After the initial tough climb, the grade eases and you traverse a north-facing slope where the cooler temperatures allow for evergreens like Douglas Fir and Ponderosa Pines. Mile 3.4-4.2: The Last Push The last mile to the summit is steep and tough, especially if you’re not used to the altitude. Take your time and take breaks. Miles 4.2-8.4: The Descent The 4.2-mile descent is harder than most hikers expect. Focusing on footing the whole way down on steep, rocky terrain is tiring, and the constant downhill impact hits the knees. Trekking poles help a lot on this stretch.

item.title: Valley of the Moon Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.22
Valley of the Moon Trail (Anza-Borrego) Updated July 2026 Jump to a section Granite monoliths rise from barren desert floor in Anza-Borrego’s remote Jacumba Wilderness, near the US-Mexico border, where the Valley of the Moon Trail delivers complete solitude and mixed cell coverage, expect limited service. Bring a satellite communicator, plenty of water, and expect to navigate terrain that most hikers never see. - Distance - 9 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 1700 ft - Time - 4–6 hrs The Valley of the Moon Trail offers a unique desert hike through some spectacular granite formations near the U.S.-Mexico border. Along the way, there’s a smugglers’ cave, abandoned mines, and a stretch of trail right on the border. It’s remote, rugged, and underrated. Video Trailhead Use this trailhead address: 48549 Old Hwy 80, Jacumba Hot Springs, CA 91934 Info There is no fee to park here. Gear Valley of the Moon Trail is in an environment of extremes. In the summer, it can be over 100°F, and when it’s cold, the wind chill can push temperatures below freezing. Check the weather link at the start of the guide to make sure you’re prepared for the conditions - and for them to change. If it’s too hot, don’t go. - Bring your backcountry essentials. - Most of the area has cell reception. At some point you may even connect to cell towers in Mexico. If you have a satellite communicator it’s prudent to bring it along. - Bring at least 2L of water, more if it’s very hot.
