We could be looking at the first hint of pandemonium for everything from airline reservations to concert tickets, or any other frustrating customer-service situation. As one person on X put it, what’s the wildest hack AI has discovered so far? It could be cutting in line.

item.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT desktop app for Linux
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.62
ChatGPT is on desktops across the world, but there’s been one place where it’s been lacking: the Linux community. Certain sectors of the open source developer community have been clamoring for OpenAI to bring its chatbot to their neck of the woods. As of this week, OpenAI has rectified this oversight, launching a dedicated ChatGPT app for Linux. “Linux has been one of the most-requested platforms for the desktop app, and this launch extends ChatGPT and Codex across every major desktop operating system,” the company said Tuesday. The new app, which is being released in preview, will give Linux users the ability to use ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex on a number of different distributions. The release is worldwide, as of Tuesday. OpenAI says that the distros that will be supported include desktop variants of Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 LTS, Debian 13, and Fedora 43 and 44. The totality of the Linux community comprises hundreds of distributions, although the distros that OpenAI has chosen here act as the base for a variety of “downstream” desktop distros or “flavors,” which should also be compatible with OpenAI’s apps as a result. OpenAI is a little behind Anthropic, which released a Claude desktop app for Linux about a month ago. Anthropic’s app is available for Ubuntu 22.04 or later and Debian 12 or later.

item.title: Anthropic says it will watermark text generated by its AI models
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.59
Anthropic will watermark text generated by its models, including Claude, to comply with European regulations, the company now says. The AI model maker confirmed the watermarking in an updated support page. EU AI Act’s Transparency Code, which took effect on August 2, requires AI companies to mark AI-generated or edited content in a way other systems can identify them. Anthropic said that all models released after August 2 will automatically have tech to watermark both computer-generated text and files. For files, the company is using the C2PA open standard. The company said it will extend support for older models as well, adding that the watermark will travel when users copy and paste the text. “Because the watermark is part of the text, it will travel with the text when it’s copied and pasted elsewhere, and may persist through some editing. Watermarking will be applied at the model level, which means it will be present no matter which Claude product or surface the text comes from,” the support page reads. It’s not clear how much editing users need to do to remove the watermark. We have asked Anthropic to clarify and will update the story if we hear back. The company noted that watermarking will apply to different products like Claude platform API, Claude, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and Claude Tag. Platforms are now rushing to watermark AI-generated content after backlash from users and to avoid regulatory scrutiny. Last week, AI music platform Suno said it will mark tracks created on its platform after a spate of legal challenges. Last month, newsletter service Substack teamed up with Pangram to flag AI-generated content. The company’s CEO, Chris Best, called out Claudefishing, a term used for people using AI to generate content. Apart from Anthropic, other companies like Black Forest Labs, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Synthesia have committed to adhering to the EU’s code.

item.title: What’s Scaleup Europe, the $5.7B fund that just backed satellite company ICEYE?
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.53
Forget the European summer lull: Startups can’t afford to stay still, and Brussels is following suit. In the middle of peak vacation time, the European Commission announced that the Scaleup Europe Fund was fully operational, with investments “expected in the coming weeks.” But its first deal was actually made public the very next day. ICEYE, a Finnish satellite intelligence company now valued above $11 billion, is the first startup backed by this unique public-private vehicle, which co-led its Series F. Similar deals should follow soon; Scaleup Europe plans to deploy €5 billion ($5.7 billion) into growth-stage startups based in the EU or partnering countries and operating in strategic sectors. “Space-based intelligence is becoming critical infrastructure for governments, and the Scaleup Europe Fund exists so companies like ours don’t have to leave Europe to compete globally,” ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski (pictured above) wrote on LinkedIn. Even in less critical sectors, helping Europe build scaleups and keep them is key for its competitiveness and tech sovereignty — and that’s also the fund’s raison d’être. With the conviction that Europe misses out when its deep tech talent lacks late-stage funding or only finds it abroad, the Commission took the matter into its own hands, but it also partnered up. Unlike other programs that are managed directly by European institutions and handing out public monies, Scaleup Europe is backed by private investors and run by Swedish asset manager EQT, which was selected via an open call to “experienced fund managers.” Other candidates reportedly included Eurazeo, Northzone, and Vitruvian Partners, with Atomico as final challenger. While it has offices across Europe, the firm may have been hindered by having its headquarters in London. But having pointed out the growth funding gap for years, still described Scaleup Europe as “urgent and necessary” when EQT was announced as the winner. As for EQT, it described the initiative as a “big moment for Europe.” “Europe has proven its ability to create successful early-stage technology companies, the challenge is now to scale those businesses into becoming global leaders while maintaining their European roots,” EQT CEO and managing partner Per Franzén commented in a statement. Notably, the Commission has given the fund manager some leeway as to where to invest — with a mandate “including but not limited to deep tech, life sciences, clean tech, advanced manufacturing, and digital technologies.” For EQT, this will overlap with the likes of AI, biotech, energy, robotics, semiconductors, and space — as shown by ICEYE. With ties to the Wallenberg family, which was initially listed as a potential anchor investor of the fund, EQT was arguably a front runner to run Scaleup Europe. With more than $300 million in assets under management, it will also be tasked with helping the fund reach its total fundraising target — starting with a “significant commitment” of its own capital. It is unclear how much capital Scaleup Europe has raised so far, but its first closing was anchored by a €1 billion investment from the Commission (approximately $1.15 billion) investing alongside institutional investors from all across Europe, credited as “founding investors.” According to public information, these founding investors include German insurance giant Allianz; APG, representing Dutch pension fund ABP; Spanish bank-affiliated funds CriteriaCaixa and Santander-owned Mouro Capital; Italy’s Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo, Intesa Sanpaolo, and Fondazione Cariplo; and Denmark’s EIFO and Novo Holdings. Scaleup Europe’s fundraising is expected to extend into 2027, with a second fundraising round described as potentially open to non-European investors, as long as these are aligned with Scaleup Europe’s objectives. This might be a necessary compromise to raise the kind of capital Scaleup Europe is seeking. According to reports, the Commission suggested it could eventually expand to €25 billion ($28.9 billion). If it does, it would start belonging to the same category as Asian and U.S. growth funds. As it stands, Scaleup Europe’s €5 billion target already makes it an outlier in the EU — VC firms in continental Europe typically manage millions, rarely billions. But with the EIF’s European Tech Champions Initiative actively backing growth-stage VC firms as a fund-of-funds, this could quickly change. In other words, Scaleup Europe may soon just be there to fill the gap.

item.title: Uber and Pony.ai plan to bring 2,000 robotaxis to Europe
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.43
Chinese autonomous vehicle maker Pony.ai and Uber plan to bring 2,000 robotaxis to four cities in Europe as part of an expanded partnership. The announcement illustrates the growing ambitions of both companies to carve out market share in the nascent robotaxi industry. Uber has partnered with more than 30 autonomous vehicle companies, including Pony.ai, over the past several years. Pony.ai, meanwhile, has launched in four Chinese cities and has locked in partnerships with local transportation authorities in an effort to bring its robotaxis to European and Middle Eastern countries, including Qatar. Uber and Pony.ai didn’t share a timeline for when these robotaxis would be deployed, or name the cities in which they’d launch, only saying that details would be revealed in phases. The companies’ now-expanded partnership does appear to have cleared up some of the terms, with Pony.ai’s “joint-deployment model” getting a clearer path to commercial scale. This means that the Guangzhou, China-based company will supply the autonomous vehicle technology, while Uber will provide its vast ride-hailing platform. Fleet management, which would include maintenance, cleaning, and charging, can be handled by a local provider, according to the companies, and the robotaxi fleet may be owned by different partners depending on the market. Uber and Pony.ai first partnered in May 2025 with a focus on the Middle East. Earlier this year, Uber and Pony.ai turned to Europe and announced plans to launch a commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb, Croatia with local company Verne.

item.title: Google’s Gemini app surges to 1 billion users
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.39
In a significant milestone for Google, CEO Sundar Pichai announced via X that the Gemini app has become one of the company’s fastest-growing products, recently surpassing 1 billion monthly active users. Pichai also noted it was the 14th Google product to hit the 1 billion mark. With this rapid growth, Gemini is keeping pace with OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which hit 1 billion monthly active users back in June. The company has been steadily integrating Gemini across its products, from Search and Workspace to Android and its standalone app. Google’s AI Mode in Search, in particular, has achieved a lot of success, with over 1 billion monthly active users globally. But today’s figure refers specifically to the Gemini app, and does not include AI users from other channels. The company also continued rolling out new models and features, including Gemini 3.5 Flash, which Google says is designed to improve coding and autonomous AI-agent tasks. Google also shared numbers of how people are actually using the chatbot, with 63% of Gemini users talking directly to the assistant using the voice feature. Plus, Gemini now generates more than 150 million images every day, according to Google. And Gemini’s growth isn’t limited to Google’s own products. The company says it now has more than 100 million active users on iOS. The milestone comes right after its Q2 2026 earnings call, where the company celebrated having over 950 million monthly users, with daily active users tripling this past year. The announcement also comes ahead of its Made by Google event, where it’s expected to have more Gemini-powered features launching across Pixel devices.

item.title: Reservoir raises $8M to make water heaters that people — and the grid — will actually want
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.31
It’s hard to imagine a home appliance more forgotten — yet more consequential — than the water heater. Most people only think of water heaters when their shower runs cold, but they represent about 18% of a household’s total energy budget and are one of the main causes of residential water damage. To Luke Winston-Almanzar, water heaters are in clear need of an upgrade. “The typical water heater is devoid of intelligence, it’s using a god-awful amount of energy, and my air fryer is smarter than it,” he told TechCrunch. “I was using more energy to heat my water than it takes to drive my electric car.” So Winston-Almanzar, who was previously chief business officer at 3D-printing startup Formlabs, co-founded Reservoir along with Gabriel Parisi-Amon and Jake Felser to make a water heater that they would want to buy. Reservoir announced Wednesday that it has raised $8 million in a seed round led by Asymmetric Capital Partners with participation from Founder Collective and MCJ. The funding will help the company install more of its water heaters in homes around the Boston area, its initial market. Reservoir has installed about 100 devices to date, and Winston-Almanzar said his company hopes to have around 1,000 installed by the end of next year. “That’s when you start talking about a megawatt-scale in terms of capacity,” he said. Storing megawatt-hours of energy as hot water could go a long way to stabilizing the grid. Today’s water heaters tend to be dumb devices, responding only to changes in temperature in the tank. But Reservoir, by predicting when people will need hot water, can heat the tank when electricity demand is low and prices are cheap. Plus, the device’s heat pump is nearly four times more efficient than an electric water heater and five times more efficient than a natural gas version. The startup has been able to show that it can relieve strain on the grid at the neighborhood level, Winston-Almanzar said. Eventually, Reservoir could aggregate its fleet of water heaters to participate in utility demand response programs, which pay handsomely for large users to avoid tapping the grid at certain times. Winston-Almanzar said he’s looking at ways to use those payments to keep Reservoir’s prices down. While energy storage might get grid experts excited, it won’t sell many water heaters. Most people replace their water heaters with whatever their plumber has on hand. The Reservoir team knew they needed to do more than build another heat pump water heater. “The sustainable product need to just be the better product,” he said. To make an appliance that customers will seek out, Reservoir has included a number of features that aren’t found in typical water heaters. The predictive heating feature ties in with energy storage. Reservoir’s water heater will spend the first month in a home gathering information about water usage patterns to train a model. Once trained, it will run the unit’s heat pump at the most efficient and cost-effective times to save money while also ensuring ample supply. Reservoir also added an ultrasonic flow sensor to help detect plumbing leaks throughout the home, sending homeowners an alert through its app. In the Max version, Reservoir added more features, including a recirculation valve to provide instant hot water and a mixing valve that can prevent pipes from freezing in cold snaps. In the Max version, a 50-gallon tank can deliver up to 150 gallons of hot water in “party mode,” which can be set either on the device’s touchscreen or through the app. To keep pricing simple and to speed up the sales process, Reservoir has also started its own plumbing company. Winston-Almanzar said that decision was inspired by his experience at Formlabs. “We built direct relationships [there] because, in a lot of cases, distributors weren’t embracing the new technology.” Reservoir’s “Max” version costs $6,500, while the base “Core” version costs $5,000, installation costs included. Massachusetts residents qualify for a $1,050 rebate, bringing the price down significantly. At $3,950, the Core model is competitive with or cheaper than existing heat pump water heaters. For comparison, the 80-gallon AO Smith that’s sitting in my basement currently costs about $3,500, and installation would add about $1,000. Traditional electric water heaters might cost less up front, at about $1,700 for an 80-gallon tank. But Winston-Almanzar said a Reservoir would save typical Boston homeowners up to $1,000 per year in energy costs. Breakeven should happen long before the Reservoir dies since the company offers a 10-year warranty. “We don’t think it’s enough just to have great technology. We think it needs to be affordable,” Winston-Almanzar said. Water heating is ripe for some new technology. The newest advance, heat pump water heaters, have failed to make a dent, commanding a small part of the market. If Reservoir succeeds, it might finally push them into the mainstream — and in the process take some pressure off the grid.

item.title: Kyoto Fusioneering starts work on key fusion power plant device
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.31
In the fusion power world, most of the attention gets lavished on the reactors themselves, where atoms fuse to unleash enormous amounts of energy. But a fusion reactor can’t run for long without a lot of other equipment, and building a fusion reactor is expensive enough on its own. Plenty of startups are happy to let someone else handle the rest. Among the dozens of companies in the emerging fusion-power supply chain, few specialists are bigger than Kyoto Fusioneering. The Japan-based company has raised $121 million in committed capital, according to FusionX. Now it has landed grants from the U.S. Department of Energy and the state of Tennessee to build a prototype fuel breeding device at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). Alongside the announcement, Kyoto Fusioneering exclusively told TechCrunch that it’s moving its U.S. headquarters to Oak Ridge. The startup has emerged as a key player in the fusion power industry. Over half of fusion startups have said they plan to work with external suppliers like Kyoto Fusioneering on fuel cycle technologies, according to a recent Fusion Industry Association survey. Kyoto Fusioneering’s forthcoming device, called Unity-3, is being developed with ORNL and will test a fuel cycle technology known as a breeding blanket. Breeding blankets harvest energy from the fusion reactor while also generating fresh fusion fuel. One breeding blanket design will use liquid lithium, which will absorb both heat and neutrons. As the lithium atoms in the blanket are bombarded with neutrons, they split into helium and tritium, an isotope of hydrogen that’s an important fuel for many reactor designs. The tritium is then separated from the blanket and sent to the reactor, while heat is extracted to generate power. All of this requires heat-resistant materials, bespoke pumps, and other specialized equipment, and it’s just one slice of a fusion power plant that needs to be developed before it can connect to the grid. Kyoto Fusioneering is also developing systems to heat fusion fuel into a plasma, recycle unburned fuel from the exhaust, and harvest heat to generate electricity. Unity-3 will test the performance of not just liquid lithium, but a range of other breeding blanket materials, Kyoto Fusioneering told TechCrunch. The device will help researchers and startups validate the data they’ve been generating, so far mostly through computer models. Other fusion startups, including Realta Fusion, Thea Energy, Type One Energy, and Xcimer Energy, will use data from the Unity-3 experiments to design their reactors. It’s a range of startups — and approaches to fusion power — that should help position Kyoto Fusioneering as a go-to supplier when fusion power is ready for the grid.

item.title: Aptoide becomes the first rival app store to return to Google Play in the US
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.28
Competing Android app stores are now back on Google Play in the U.S., and Aptoide is the first to take advantage of the new option. On Monday, the Portugal-based app distributor brought its games store back to Google Play after more than a decade, crediting the loosening of restrictions that had been criticized as anticompetitive. For the first time in many years, U.S. users will be able to install a competitor to Google’s Android app store directly from Google Play itself, a milestone in terms of opening the app market to more competition. Aptoide’s independent app store is one of the larger Android app marketplaces outside of Google Play, offering more than 40,000 Android applications to its roughly 25 million monthly active users. The U.S. has been Aptoide’s largest market to date, but until now, the store had to be sideloaded on Android devices, limiting its reach. That changed following U.S. District Judge James Donato’s ruling in the Epic Games lawsuit, which, among other things, now requires Google to allow the installation of third-party apps from outside the Play Store. As of June 22, 2026, Google began allowing third-party app stores to access Google Play’s app catalog through the Play Catalog Access Program. This allows competitors to access Google Play infrastructure, including its catalog of apps that can be offered to users, while remaining an independent store. Epic Games first sued Google in 2020, alleging anticompetitive abuses in the Android app ecosystem. A jury trial ruled in Epic’s favor in 2023. Google appealed the ruling, but lost. Earlier this year, the company said it would drop Play Store commissions and make it easier for Android users to install alternative app stores.

item.title: India’s Yulu raises $93M as quick-commerce boom fuels e-bike demand
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.20
As India’s quick-commerce platforms race to deliver everything from groceries to smartphones in minutes, electric mobility startup Yulu has seized the boom, raising $93 million in fresh funding. The Bengaluru‑based startup offers electric two‑wheelers on weekly subscription plans, so delivery drivers can jump straight into the gig economy without buying their own vehicles. With around 50,000 vehicles in its fleet, Yulu reports that it logs about 1.6 million zero‑emission miles each week and powers more than 750,000 deliveries a day. The new funding will let Yulu grow that fleet to 200,000 bikes over the next two years and launch faster electric two-wheelers aimed at new logistics use cases. The Series C round comprised $63 million in equity led by GEF Capital Partners and $30 million in debt financing. About $5.5 million of the equity component was used to buy shares from seed investors whose funds were nearing the end of their investment life, co-founder and CEO Amit Gupta said in an interview. The deal valued Yulu at about $170 million post-money, people familiar with the matter told TechCrunch. Gupta declined to comment when asked about the valuation and did not dispute the figure. Existing investors Bajaj Auto and Magna International did not participate in the round after waiving their pre-emptive rights, allowing GEF to acquire its target ownership stake, Gupta said. He added that the startup expects this to be its final equity fundraising before an eventual public listing, with future fleet expansion financed primarily through debt and lease financing. The business moves toward becoming profitable before interest and taxes next year, after achieving positive EBITDA last financial year, Gupta told TechCrunch. The startup also grew its revenue seven-fold between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, he said, without sharing specifics. The COVID shift Founded as a bike-sharing startup for urban commuters in 2017, Yulu found its biggest opportunity during the COVID-19 pandemic as demand for food and grocery deliveries accelerated. Today, Gupta told TechCrunch that about 95% of Yulu’s revenue comes from renting electric bikes to gig workers on weekly subscriptions, while the rest is generated by its station‑based rental service in Bengaluru. The startup has also dropped an earlier plan to sell bikes directly to consumers. To fuel its next growth phase, Yulu is introducing a full-sized, higher‑speed electric scooter, called Yulu Express. It is designed for longer‑haul e‑commerce deliveries, bike taxis, and express parcel services — areas that its slower fleet could not previously cover. About a third of the planned 200,000‑vehicle fleet will be made up of this new model, Gupta said. While Yulu’s current low‑speed fleet is built by Bajaj Auto, the new high‑speed scooter comes from a different Indian manufacturer that Gupta declined to name. About 500 of the new bikes are already running in Bengaluru and are being trialed in three additional cities, Gupta told TechCrunch. Currently, Yulu operates in 12 Indian cities, running its own operations in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi‑NCR, and Hyderabad, while partnering with franchisees in eight other markets. The startup, Gupta said, aims to reach roughly 20 cities within the next year, with Chennai and Pune among the key targets for expansion. Gupta stated that Yulu partners with almost every major quick‑commerce, food‑delivery, and e‑commerce platform — including Amazon and Walmart-owned Flipkart — though its customers are the gig workers who rent the bikes, not the platforms themselves. He compared Yulu’s role to “the AWS of mobility,” supplying the infrastructure that lets delivery workers operate without any third-party logistics providers taking a cut.

item.title: The Trouble With Trying to Turn Viral Videos Into Blockbusters
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 5.33
Almost 14 years ago, the producer Scott Glassgold stumbled on a short film on Vimeo about a woman who believes she’s encountered an alien. The project, by a pair of filmmakers named Zeek Earl and Chris Caldwell, was “a wonderful, lo-fi science-fiction story” that conveyed a distinct storytelling voice, Glassgold told me. He immediately set out to work with them, hoping to introduce the pair to Hollywood as fresh directing talent. “That was an early moment for me on the internet,” he explained. “I just saw it as an incredibly viable path to meeting artists, finding ideas, frankly, in a place where, at the time, really no one else was looking.” He learned from that period, however, that Hollywood wasn’t universally enthusiastic about turning such material into feature-length movies—at least, not with unknown, internet-bred creators involved. Even though Earl and Caldwell’s work attracted potential studio buyers, Glassgold sought independent financing to help the pair avoid what’s known in the industry as development hell. “The first call I would get from a studio head would be like, We’re so excited. When can we fire the director?” Glassgold recalled. “I would just put my hands on my face, because it was entirely antithetical to what we were trying to achieve.” That was, as Glassgold put it, “the 1.0” of Hollywood’s dalliance with the internet—a far cry from the industry’s upgraded view of digital-native talent these days. Works by filmmakers who first found success online consistently scored at the box office this spring: Backrooms, directed by Kane Parsons, who went viral as a teenager with a web series set in the same world of liminal spaces, is now the studio A24’s highest-grossing movie ever. Obsession, a horror-comedy made by Curry Barker, who first built an audience on YouTube through sketch-comedy videos, became a word-of-mouth hit. And Iron Lung, a video-game adaptation self-financed, directed, and released by the gaming YouTuber known as Markiplier, grossed at least 10 times its budget worldwide with the help of his nearly 40 million subscribers. Hollywood, inspired by these triumphs, is doing what it does best: working overtime to capture the same magic again. Several projects with online roots have recently entered into development to become feature-length films, including Siren Head and Cartoon Cat, each inspired by the disturbing viral imagery of the artist Trevor Henderson; Seasons, an adaptation of a short story first published on the Subreddit r/nosleep, a forum for grassroots horror writing, about a couple whose dream ranch turns out to be haunted; and The Mandela Catalogue, a script based, much like Backrooms, on a popular horror series on YouTube. Mandela, set in a fictional county in Wisconsin that’s invaded by shape-shifting creatures, led to an 11-studio bidding war, with Steven Spielberg signing on as a producer along the way. Aaron B. Koontz, an indie filmmaker and a producer for Mandela, told me that Hollywood’s new fascination with digital creators has been vindicating—and overwhelming. “It’s the opposite of what I’m used to in my entire career,” he said, adding that after Backrooms’ release, he was on the phone every day for three weeks with executives interested in picking up Mandela. “People in Hollywood that never took my call,” he said, “are now calling me.” To the filmmaker Shawn Levy, whose production company 21 Laps worked on Backrooms and Seasons, these green-lighted projects merely underline “a predictable sort of frenzy” based on the latest Hollywood success story; they’re not a sure sign that the industry is shifting significantly. “Even though right now there’s a mad gold rush of assistants being tasked with scouring the internet for the next Kane Parsons or the next Curry,” he told me, “most long-shot bets don’t pan out.” Hollywood has clearly grasped that the next auteurs and franchises can be found on the web. “Nothing teaches Hollywood a faster lesson than a hit,” Levy said. But whether Hollywood’s intensive focus on all things internet leads to anything resembling this year’s box-office successes will depend on the industry seeing the internet as more than just a place from which to mine ideas. Hollywood once seemed baffled by the internet. Throughout the 2010s, almost every time the industry attempted to translate trendy web culture into conventional entertainment, the results were largely forgettable: The Grumpy Cat meme inexplicably starred in a Lifetime holiday movie, a thread about one writer’s father’s curmudgeonly sayings became a quickly canceled sitcom, and a major studio’s adaptation of Slender Man, a character that originated on an internet forum, bombed with critics. Yet over the years, the language of digital natives began to influence popular culture anyway as the internet became intertwined with daily life. Consider the growing slate of satires about influencers, the numerous coming-of-age films that have tapped into teenage angst amid the rise of social media, and the fact that entire movies have been made that take place exclusively on computer screens. TikTok users embraced Skinamarink, an experimental horror flick made for 15,000 Canadian dollars, by posting story breakdowns and their terrified live reactions. The director Jane Schoenbrun’s films—including their latest, Teenage Sex and Death in Camp Miasma—could be considered an offshoot of internet culture, trafficking as they do in esoteric online-fandom sensibilities. Their movies, packed with surreal imagery and dream-logic-driven plots, conjure the sensation of getting lost down an internet rabbit hole. The road to building such an oeuvre, however, required “lying,” Schoenbrun told me with a laugh. When they were pitching their projects to traditional studio brass, many of the executives they met didn’t understand the stories at first glance, even though they sought voices like Schoenbrun’s. “It’s like,” the director explained, “trying to say something in a way that will be understood and digestible.” That kind of code-switching can create tension, according to Lucas Ford, a producer I spoke with. He would know: As an assistant at 21 Laps in early 2022, Ford brought Parsons’s YouTube channel to the attention of Levy and his fellow executive Dan Cohen. Today, Ford runs his own production company, translating ideas from all kinds of visual artists and writers into potential films. He told me that when pitching to studios, he tries to go beyond highlighting shallow metrics—viewer counts, subscriber numbers—and instead articulate why he’s personally drawn to the material. Any internet creator who has built an online following has a relationship with their audience that Hollywood should cultivate rather than erase, Ford noted; if a movie adapting an online work has forced its digital-native storyteller’s vision to fit conventional molds, viewers familiar with the original material “can sniff that out immediately.” Schoenbrun told me something similar, observing that Backrooms and Obsession had brought young people to theaters by appealing to their concerns about, say, the flagging economy and dating habits. “This was youth culture speaking to itself,” they said of those films. By offering more internet talent a chance to bring their visions to big-screen life, Hollywood seems eager to further invoke today’s youth culture. But deepening that relationship, Levy said, will require precise care. He told me that he’d initially had “healthy skepticism” about Backrooms’ ability to become a feature-length film: “Certainly, question marks abounded,” he explained, including “the fact that it was a teenager who was being given the keys to the car.” In the end, he pushed the movie forward; he trusted his team’s assessment of both the concept and, after meeting him, Parsons’s capacity to turn an aesthetic into a fleshed-out story deserving of a theatrical release. Adapting this kind of material can require different approaches. Koontz, the Mandela Catalogue producer, told me that he’d advocated for its creator, Alex Kister, to direct and co-write the film adaptation because a large part of the project’s appeal came from Kister’s creative flourishes: He uses alternating points of view, plenty of biblical allusions, even footage from a children’s cartoon. For Siren Head, though, Glassgold explained that the material warranted bringing experienced filmmakers on board. Henderson’s artwork, as striking as it is, isn’t enough of a foundation for a movie, so the film is moving forward with two Hollywood-horror veterans overseeing its creation: the screenwriter Brian Duffield and the Weapons director Zach Cregger, who are collaborating on the script. The internet has never been predictable: Backrooms’, Obsession’s, and Iron Lung’s collective overperformance at the box office argues against the kind of gold-rush thinking that is driving Hollywood to seek out digital storytellers. Even for the filmmakers who achieved liftoff from their online beginnings, the web can be an unreliable foundation on which to build. Kyle Edward Ball, the director of Skinamarink, told me that he began uploading videos on YouTube in the 2010s in part because he believed that going viral would help launch his career. He instead found the platform more useful as a training ground, honing his voice one video at a time. (Ball noticed at the time that amassing views certainly led some creators to Hollywood success, but many of the results seemed to involve “bedazzling the wheel instead of reinventing it,” he said.) Schoenbrun, for their part, pointed out that the flurry of headlines about digital-native talent impressing Hollywood has tended to flatten anything that began on the internet into one genre, despite the fact that, creatively, Backrooms isn’t Obsession, just as Siren Head won’t resemble The Mandela Catalogue. The artists behind these works also approach the internet differently; Parsons riffed on an aesthetic born on internet forums, for instance, while Barker treated online behavior as his subject matter. (His first feature film, Milk & Serial, is about YouTube pranksters.) Hollywood’s latest fixation could be just a brief, reductive detour away from tentpole franchises or superhero films and into horror movies (one of the most reliable genres for producing mainstream hits) that take nontraditional paths to being made. “I’m not like, Wow, this is the French New Wave for YouTube, you know?” Schoenbrun said. Maybe not, yet the film industry does seem to have hit the jackpot—these few times, at least—in a realm that has long appeared to confound it. Either way, Ball told me, it’s a thrilling moment for artists bred online to experiment without worrying about fitting any filmmaking molds. “Don’t chase Hollywood,” he said. “Have Hollywood chase you.”

item.title: Katendrecht: Rotterdam’s sailors’ quarter reinvented as cultural hub
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 5.36
Why go now? A thin peninsula just south of Rotterdam’s centre, Katendrecht was once at the heart of the world’s busiest port, home to continental Europe’s first Chinatown and a lively sailors’ quarter. Its later reputation as a red light district has been shrugged off – part of the city’s wider reinvention in the aftermath of extensive second world war bombing. Still Europe’s largest port, Rotterdam’s maritime history is very much evident today, with the former headquarters of the Holland-America Line now a hotel just a short hop across the Rijnhaven Bridge. The 2012 opening of this pedestrian and bicycle bridge finally connected cut-off Katendrecht to Wilhelminapier, which was a jumping off point for transatlantic migration, and is today a major cruise terminal, with more than 100 ships departing every year. The opening of the Fenix museum of migration last year and the reopening of the Nederlands Fotomuseum in a new location here in February have accelerated Katendrecht’s rise in status, following on from the entrepreneurs and creatives who have introduced craft breweries, food halls and design boutiques in recent years. Former warehouses have been transformed – into the aforementioned museums among other venues – and a lively cultural and arts scene has grown as the neighbourhood has seen new residents rediscover the formerly downtrodden area. With more big construction projects under way, Katendrecht will be transformed further over the next five years, with apartments, shops, a five-star hotel, an urban beach and, notably, the Rotterdam Centre for Dance, Danshuis, on the horizon. Where to eat and drink Deliplein is the place to begin – the tree-lined square lies at the heart of the old sailors’ quarter and houses more than 20 restaurants and bars. Originally home to the first Chinese restaurant in the Netherlands, Delistraat is buzzing from morning to night. Start at Jordy’s Bakery, where flaky pastries, vegan muffins, sourdough sandwiches and speciality coffees will fuel you for the morning. Across the road in the Fenix atrium, O: Anatolian Café is run by the Michelin-starred chef Maksut Aşkar; on the menu are all-day Turkish breakfasts, meze platters, sandwiches and salads at extremely reasonable prices. Kaapse Brouwers in the Fenix Food Factory is where the post-work crowd heads. Sit on the terrace, admire the waterfront view and explore its range of more than 20 craft beers on tap – from Belgian blonds and New England IPAs to pilsners and sours. And back on Delistraat, Café de Ouwehoer is a classic old-style pub with a nod to the area’s past – and a huge range of whiskeys to boot. A few doors down, finish your evening at the small but perfectly formed fine-dining establishment De Matroos en Het Meisje (The Sailor and the Girl), which offers a changing daily menu. With the option of choosing from four to six courses, dependent on season and produce, dishes could be charred carrot, cured Japanese fish, creme fraiche and onion, or chicken breast with mushroom beurre blanc, blackberries and crisped rice. Cultural experiences Fenix is the obvious first stop. Funded by the philanthropic foundation Droom en Daad (Dream and Do), the museum of immigration opened last May in a renovated historic warehouse and finally gave Katendrecht a real focal point for visitors. Formerly part of the world’s largest warehouse for cargo transfer, the museum reflects the fact that millions of migrants arrived at and departed from the port in search of a new life. At its heart is the Tornado, a spectacular mirrored spiral staircase, which offers 360-degree views across the neighbourhood, docks and the city. It symbolises the central theme, with architect Ma Yansong describing it as “a metaphor for the journeys of migrants”. The industrial space is used sparingly to display photography, art and sculpture that communicate the experience of immigration, movement and displacement of peoples. It’s humbling and moving. The exhibition All Directions features more than 100 artists, with stories of the war in Kyiv and refugee camps in Tunisia, Jordan and Lebanon, as well as a lifesize New York bus made from fabric. The Family of Migrants exhibition showcases more than 200 photos from around the world, depicting the story of migration from the late 19th century to the present day. And the Suitcase Labyrinth has about 2,000 donated cases, dating from 1898 to today, with 30 audio stories detailing the unique past of some of them. Farther down the waterfront, the newly opened Nederlands Fotomuseum is also in a renovated warehouse – formerly used to store coffee from Brazil – and is topped with a modern anodised aluminium structure. Inside, the exposed brick, rough-edged concrete and steel girders offer a striking contrast to the impressive photography on display. The original museum opened in 2003, and the collection now comprises more than six million negatives, transparencies, prints, photo albums and other archival matter – visitors are encouraged to look in the depots and studios. Every week, thousands of images are digitised and made available online, while old and damaged photography is conserved and restored. On the first floor, the Gallery of Honour of Dutch Photography showcases 99 distinguished photographs, selected by a group of experts, spanning 1842 to the digital era. And as you go up the central staircase, which leads all the way to the rooftop restaurant, a mosaic of projected images merely hints at the breadth and depth of photography in storage. Where to shop In the Bay House development, close to the Nederlands Fotomuseum, there are a number of designer fashion and vintage furniture stores. Selected With Love has “upcycled” clothing, Caesar sells designer menswear, while The Gallery by Collectors Network is a space for numerous independent dealers selling vintage design pieces – Vintage Hoarder, for example, has 1980s Belgian floor lamps, a 1970s French slate table and 1960s Italian dining chairs. The museum shops offer the best range of unique purchases. Fenix has items created in collaboration with artists and designers as well as chocolates from Rotterdam, slippers from Greece and tea from small family-run plantations in China. Don’t miss Verhalenhuis Belvédère is perhaps the best place to get a sense of where Katendrecht has come from. Dating from 1894, the building was originally a cafe then a jazz club – saved from demolition, it became a cultural centre, community hub and exhibition space in 2009. As part of its cultural programmes, community meals and storytelling events, Belvédère collects and shares the stories of Rotterdam residents, from the first Cape Verdean migrants to Jewish families and Chinese seafarers. Where to stay Of Hotel New York’s 72 rooms, the suites in the former offices of the Holland-America Line’s directors, overlooking the Nieuwe Maas river, and the two tower rooms are the ones to book. Rooms from €110. On the western tip of Katendrecht, the former cruise ship SS Rotterdam is permanently moored and is now a 254-room hotel that retains much of its original styling, with wood panelling throughout, and the public spaces – bars, restaurants, theatre – are like stepping back in time. Tours are available. Rooms from €73. The five-star Eurostars hotel is expected to open in the autumn, next door to the Nederlands Fotomuseum and right by the Rijnhaven metro station, which connects easily to Rotterdam Centraal train station. The trip was hosted by the Netherlands Board of Tourism & Conventions

item.title: American Express adds more than 350 hotels to Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.55
American Express adds more than 350 hotels to Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection In celebration of its 35th anniversary, American Express Travel is expanding its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs to include more than 350 new properties worldwide. Fine Hotels + Resorts launched in 1991 with just 120 properties. Today, the additions bring the combined portfolio to more than 3,400 properties across 116 countries, including hotels in destinations such as Japan, New Zealand, Morocco and Argentina. The expansion gives eligible American Express cardholders more properties to choose from when booking through Amex Travel. Here's what cardmembers should know. What new hotels are joining Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection? American Express has added 351 properties to its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection collections. The new additions span destinations in Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania and South America. Most are already bookable on AmexTravel.com, with a small handful to be made available in the coming days. Here are a few of the hotels joining the programs: - Casa Lucia, Melia Collection in Buenos Aires, Argentina - ESPACIO Nagoya Castle in Nagoya, Japan - Fontainebleau Miami Beach in Miami Beach, Florida - Moana Surfrider, A Westin Resort & Spa in Honolulu, Hawaii - One&Only Moonlight Basin in Big Sky, Montana - Park Hyatt Cabo del Sol in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico - ROKI Queenstown in Queenstown, New Zealand - Selman Marrakech in Marrakech, Morocco - Six Senses London in London, United Kingdom - The Lake Como EDITION in Cadenabbia, Italy The expansion adds properties across a range of destinations and travel styles, including beach getaways, city stays, wellness-focused trips and adventure destinations. "Our Hotel Curation Team reviews each property against a set of required and preferred criteria informed by what we know our premium Card Members value when they travel," Audrey Hendley, president of American Express Travel, told TPG. Hendley said the assessment ultimately determines which program is the better fit, with Fine Hotels + Resorts representing Amex's luxury hotel program and The Hotel Collection offering a curated selection of premium properties. American Express did not disclose how many properties, if any, left the programs as part of this update. Hendley said the portfolio evolves over time, with hotels joining and leaving based on factors including cardmember interest and alignment with program standards. Related: Everything you need to know about Amex Travel Which cards can access Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection? Your access to American Express' hotel programs depends on which card you have. The Hotel Collection is available to a broader range of eligible American Express cardmembers, while Fine Hotels + Resorts has a narrower eligibility list. Cardmembers with the following cards can access The Hotel Collection: - American Express Platinum Card® - The Business Platinum Card® from American Express - American Express® Gold Card - American Express® Business Gold Card - The Centurion Card from American Express (invite-only; both business and personal versions are eligible) The Hotel Collection requires a minimum stay of two consecutive nights to receive its benefits. Fewer cards qualify for Fine Hotels + Resorts: - Amex Platinum - Amex Business Platinum - The American Express Corporate Platinum Card® - The Centurion Card (invite-only; both business and personal versions are eligible) Unlike The Hotel Collection, Fine Hotels + Resorts doesn't require a two-night minimum stay to receive program benefits. The information for the Amex Corporate Platinum, Centurion and Business Centurion Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Some eligible cards also offer statement credits for hotel bookings through Amex Travel. Enrollment is required. For example, the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum offer up to $600 in annual hotel statement credits for eligible prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. The benefit is split into up to $300 in statement credits from January through June and another up to $300 from July through December. This benefit is separate from the $100 on-property credit offered as part of FHR and THC stays. Related: The best American Express cards What benefits do eligible cardholders receive? Benefits vary between Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection. With Fine Hotels + Resorts, eligible cardmembers receive: - Daily breakfast for two - A $100 credit toward eligible on-property charges (varies by property) - Guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout - Noon check-in (subject to availability) - A room upgrade upon arrival (subject to availability) - Complimentary Wi-Fi With The Hotel Collection, eligible cardmembers receive: - A $100 credit toward eligible on-property charges (varies by property) - Noon check-in (subject to availability) - 4 p.m. late checkout (subject to availability) - A room upgrade upon arrival (subject to availability) The Hotel Collection requires a stay of at least two consecutive nights to receive these benefits. Fine Hotels + Resorts doesn't have a minimum stay requirement. Eligible cardmembers booking through FHR can earn Membership Rewards points while also having the opportunity to earn points with participating hotel loyalty programs when enrolled and eligible. "When it comes to hotels specifically, we like to say 'Book Once, Earn Twice,'" Hendley said. Related: Here's your guide to the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum prepaid hotel credit Bottom line The addition of more than 350 hotels gives eligible Amex cardmembers significantly more options for booking through Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection, bringing the programs' combined footprint to more than 3,400 properties across 116 countries. Beyond providing more choices for travelers looking to take advantage of FHR and THC's on-property perks, the expansion also gives eligible Platinum cardmembers more opportunities to use their hotel statement credits.

item.title: Which United credit card is right for you? Comparing the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.19
Which United credit card is right for you? Comparing the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards If you've flown United, you've probably wondered whether you're leaving value on the table by not carrying one of the airline's cobranded credit cards. And after United's MileagePlus changes earlier this year, the answer is more likely than ever to be yes (more on that below). As a United cardholder myself, I've seen that value increase firsthand: I now earn 20% more miles on United flights than I did before the changes. But with several different United cards offering different combinations of perks, figuring out which one is right for you isn't always straightforward. United offers a range of airline cards with varying perks, from a straightforward personal option for occasional flyers to premium personal and business cards for travelers seeking lounge access and elite status. Choosing the right card comes down to how often you fly United, which perks you'll actually use and whether those benefits justify the annual fee. Here's how the United consumer and business cards compare — and how to decide which one is the best fit for your wallet. United cards at a glance: Annual fees and welcome offers Here's a quick look at each United credit card's annual fee and current welcome offer: | Card | Annual fee | Current welcome offer | |---|---|---| | | $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 | Earn up to 60,000 bonus miles: Earn 50,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening. | | | $350 | Earn up to 70,000 bonus miles and 500 PQPs: Earn 60,000 bonus miles and 500 PQPs after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening. | | | $695 | Earn up to 90,000 bonus miles: Earn 80,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening. | | | $150 | Earn up to 110,000 bonus miles and 2,000 PQPs: Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles and 2,000 PQPs after you spend $5,000 on purchases in the first three months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after you add an employee card to your account in the first three months from account opening. | United Explorer Card Best for: Occasional United flyers who want the core travel perks without a premium price tag Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 Standout perks: - A discount of at least 10% when booking flights with miles (Premier status members can save even more) - One complimentary checked bag for the primary cardmember and one companion - Priority boarding for the primary cardmember and companions on the same reservation - Two United Club℠ one-time passes per year The United Explorer Card covers the basics that matter most on a typical trip, such as a free bag, priority boarding and a couple of lounge passes, without asking you to pay a premium fee for perks you'd rarely use. It's the right fit for someone who flies United a handful of times a year and wants the card to pay for itself without overthinking it. TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak says the two United Club passes alone tend to make the card worth it for her: "A day pass into a United Club costs $59, so if I use both of my passes, I've almost entirely covered my annual fee." She adds that the 9-miles-per-dollar-spent rate on standard United fares booked with the card is the other reason it's stayed in her wallet (earning rate may vary for those with United MileagePlus status and for those flying basic economy). Compared to the United Quest Card, the Explorer is the more accessible option for less frequent flyers, while the Quest makes more sense once you're checking bags and chasing status often enough to justify the higher fee. To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer Card. Apply here: United Explorer Card United Quest Card Best for: Regular United flyers who check bags often and want a real head start toward Premier status Annual fee: $350 Standout perks: - Two complimentary checked bags for the primary cardmember and one companion - Priority boarding for the primary cardmember and companions on the same reservation - One $200 annual United travel credit - Premier Access travel services, including priority check-in, security screening and boarding where available - A discount of at least 10% when booking flights with miles (Premier status members can save even more) - An annual 10,000-mile award flight discount The United Quest Card is built for travelers who fly United often enough to want more than the free bag and priority boarding the Explorer offers — and who want a card that actively pushes them toward Premier status. Between the $200 credit and the two free checked bags, much of the $350 annual fee can be offset for anyone flying United a few times a year, especially if you prefer to check a bag rather than tow a carry-on. For example, United charges $45 for a first checked bag and $55 for a second on domestic flights (when you prepay), so checking two bags on a round-trip flight could otherwise cost $200. Take a few similar trips each year, and those savings can quickly add up. Clint Henderson, a principal spokesperson at TPG, says the $200 trip credit and elevated earning on United flights initially won him over, with "free checked bags and priority boarding" giving him reason enough to keep the card long-term. One major shortcoming of the Quest, especially compared to the lower-fee Explorer, is its lack of lounge access — as a reminder, the Explorer offers two, one-time United Club passes per year. However, it makes up for that with a more robust collection of statement credits, an annual award flight discount and an additional complimentary checked bag. While the Club Card includes enhanced perks and unlimited access to the United Club, the Quest is the better pick for flyers who can do without lounge access on every trip. To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest Card. Apply here: United Quest Card United Club Card Best for: Frequent United flyers who want lounge access Annual fee: $695 Standout perks: - Unlimited United Club access for you and a guest (a $750-plus value per year) - Free first and second checked bags for the primary cardmember and one companion on the same reservation - Priority boarding for the primary cardmember and companions on the same reservation - Premier Access travel services, including priority check-in, security screening and boarding where available - More than $875 in annual partner credits, including hotel, ride-hailing, car rental and Instacart credits - A discount of at least 10% when booking flights with miles (Premier status members can save even more) The Club Card is for travelers who treat lounge access as a need rather than a nice-to-have. The unlimited visits for two can outweigh the $695 annual fee on their own for anyone who flies regularly with a plus-one, before factoring in the checked bags, Premier Access or partner credits. Christine Gallipeau, a senior loyalty program editor at TPG, says the card's "fantastic benefits," including its complimentary United Club membership, discounted United awards and up to $150 in annual ride-hailing credits (yearly activation required), "have justified keeping the card in my wallet, especially as a frequent traveler based near United's Washington, D.C., hub." Against the Quest, the Club costs nearly double, but that gap effectively replaces what would otherwise be a separate United Club membership. Flyers who rarely set foot in a United Club are usually better served sticking with Quest's travel credit and PQP earnings instead. The Club only pulls ahead once lounge access becomes a habit rather than an occasional treat. To learn more, read our full review of the United Club Card. Apply here: United Club Card United Business Card Best for: Small-business owners and frequent United flyers who want lounge passes and perks without a premium annual fee Annual fee: $150 Standout perks: - Two United Club one-time passes per year - Complimentary first checked bag for the primary cardmember and one companion on the same reservation - Priority boarding for the primary cardmember and companions on the same reservation - $125 United travel credit (after making five United flight purchases of $100 or more each calendar year with your card) - A discount of at least 10% when booking flights with miles (Premier status members can save even more) - Elevated earning rates in common business categories, such as dining, gas stations, office supply stores, local transit and commuting The United Business Card packs a surprising amount of value into a moderate $150 annual fee, pairing a travel credit and lounge passes with a PQP boost that can meaningfully nudge business travelers toward Premier status. It carries the same annual fee as the Explorer (after the first year; the Explorer has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150), but is built for business travelers who can turn everyday business expenses into progress toward Premier status. Unlike the United Club Card, it offers just two one-time passes a year, which should be enough for someone who only wants occasional lounge access. That's part of the appeal for Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site content strategy. She says the card works particularly well alongside the United Quest Card: "That card doesn't include any lounge access, so the United Business Card fills a gap with its two United Club one-time passes per year." She also appreciates the 5,000 bonus miles she gets each anniversary for holding both cards: "It's not a ton of miles, but it's a nice reward for keeping a card combo I was going to carry anyway!" To learn more, read our full review of the United Business Card. Apply here: United Business Card How to choose the right United credit card for your travel style When choosing the right United card, it's helpful to think about how often you fly the carrier and the benefits you're looking to gain. Here's a framework to help you decide: - You fly United at least once a year and mainly want to save on baggage fees: The United Explorer Card is usually sufficient. - You check bags often and want a real shot at Premier status: The United Quest Card tends to deliver the most tangible annual value, between the travel credit and the PQP earnings. - You fly frequently and want lounge access built in: The United Club Card is built for this type of traveler, offering unlimited club visits and a deep bench of partner credits. - You run a small business and fly United regularly: The United Business Card offers a lighter-weight path to lounge passes and elite-qualifying points. What about the United Gateway and United Club Business cards? United also offers the no-annual-fee United Gateway℠ Card (see rates and fees) and premium United Club℠ Business Card, but neither made my main comparison. While the Gateway is United's only no-annual-fee card, most United flyers will get more practical value from the Explorer, which also offers no annual fee for the first year (then $150). The Explorer includes a free first checked bag for the primary cardholder and one companion, while Gateway cardholders must spend $10,000 in a calendar year to earn two free checked bags. The United Club Business Card is a more compelling option, but its $695 annual fee makes it best suited to business owners who regularly use United Clubs and can maximize the value of its collection of travel and lifestyle credits. For everyone else, the $150 United Business Card offers many of the core United benefits — including two annual Club passes and a free checked bag — at a fraction of the cost. The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Related: How to choose an airline credit card Why it's more valuable than ever to be a United cardholder It's arguably never been a better time to be a United cardholder. United MileagePlus overhauled its earning rates earlier this year, and the message was clear: cardholders and elite members come first. As of April 2, mileage-earning rates dropped across the board for members without a United card or status, while eligible cardholders can earn substantially more. A general MileagePlus member, for example, now earns 3 miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights, compared with 6 miles per dollar for a cardholder before factoring in the additional miles earned from the card itself. Basic economy fares became even less rewarding for non-cardholders, with most travelers booking those tickets no longer earning miles at all unless they hold status or an eligible cobranded card. On the flip side, cardholders now get more substantial award ticket discounts of at least 10%, with deeper savings for Premier members, stacked on top of the extra miles per dollar spent their card already provides. Altogether, the changes significantly widen the gap between United cardholders and travelers without a card or status, making a cobranded card considerably more valuable than it was before. Related: How the United Quest Card changed my airline loyalty Bottom line The best United card isn't necessarily the one with the most perks. Instead, it's the one that matches how you actually travel. Occasional flyers will likely get plenty of value from the Explorer, while frequent travelers may find the Quest or Club cards easily justify their higher annual fees. And for small-business owners, the United Business Card offers many of the same travel benefits at a lower price point. With United now rewarding cardholders more generously than ever, carrying the right cobranded card can help you save money, earn more miles and unlock a better travel experience every time you fly.

item.title: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: Which is better for Alaska and Hawaiian flyers?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.14
Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: Which is better for Alaska and Hawaiian flyers? Editor's Note Atmos Rewards is the joint loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers. While Atmos Rewards primarily targets frequent flyers of these airlines, the program offers more than meets the eye. Atmos Rewards points are among the most valuable airline miles and can be used to book flights on Oneworld partners, including American Airlines. The program offers two personal cobranded credit cards issued by Bank of America. The Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card is a solid entry-level rewards card with a $95 annual fee. Meanwhile, the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is a premium card for Alaska and Hawaiian loyalists, loaded with perks for a higher $395 annual fee. Which card is right for you? Let's dive in and see which Atmos Rewards card you should add to your wallet. Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit comparison | Card | Atmos Ascent | Atmos Summit | |---|---|---| | Annual fee | $95 | $395 | | Earning rates | | | | Welcome bonus | Earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. | Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. | | Travel perks | | | | Benefits when flying Alaska or Hawaiian | | | | Lounge perks | $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ Membership | Two Alaska Lounge passes each quarter | Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit welcome bonus Both cards provide solid welcome bonuses. New applicants for the Atmos Ascent can earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. Per TPG's August 2026 valuations, the points in this offer are worth $1,085. Meanwhile, the Atmos Summit is offering new cardholders the ability to earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. This offer is worth up to $1,628 when you combine the value of the base points and the Global Companion Award, according to TPG's valuations. Winner: Atmos Summit. Its bonus is worth more than the Atmos Ascent. Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit benefits As noted in the table above, the Atmos Ascent and Atmos Summit share some benefits, including: - One free checked bag for the cardholder and up to six other passengers on the same reservation - Preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines - 20% back on all inflight purchases The Atmos Summit has a higher $395 annual fee and more elevated perks than the entry-level Atmos Ascent, which costs $95 a year. Some benefits differ slightly, but the distinctions are important to note. Companion perks Atmos Summit cardholders receive an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award each account anniversary and can earn a 100,000-point Global Companion Award after spending at least $60,000 on the card in the prior anniversary year. Atmos Ascent cardholders receive an annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) each account anniversary after spending at least $6,000 on the card in the prior anniversary year. Lounge benefits The Atmos Summit grants two Alaska Lounge passes per quarter. To use the pass, you must be flying on a same-day ticketed Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld or partner airline flight. Meanwhile, Atmos Ascent cardholders receive $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership, which costs $795 per year and includes access to all Alaska Lounges and nearly 90 partner lounges. While the Atmos Ascent's $100 lounge membership discount is generous for the card's $95 annual fee, the lounge passes will provide significant value for those flying in or out of an airport with an Alaska Lounge at least once each quarter. Status points Atmos Summit cardholders earn 1 status point for every $2 spent on the card, with no spending cap. You'll also earn 10,000 status points each year on your account anniversary. Atmos Ascent cardholders earn 1 status point for every $3 spent on the card, with no spending cap. The Atmos Summit's 10,000 status points on each account anniversary automatically puts cardholders halfway to Atmos Silver status, the lowest tier in the program. Summit exclusive perks Finally, some perks are exclusive to the premium Atmos Summit: - No change fees when you need to make a same-day change to an Alaska flight - $50 voucher for Alaska Airlines flight cancellations or departure delays of two or more hours - Up to $120 in statement credits for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years - Two inflight Wi-Fi passes on Alaska flights per quarter These benefits are especially helpful to those who frequently fly on Alaska Airlines. Winner: Atmos Summit. For a higher annual fee, the Summit provides a faster path to elite status, more built-in perks and better benefits for those who frequently fly with Alaska, Hawaiian or partner airlines. Earning points with the Atmos Ascent vs. the Atmos Summit The Atmos Ascent and Atmos Summit both earn Atmos Rewards points. The cards share an earning rate on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, at 3 points per dollar spent. Plus, both cards earn a 10% rewards bonus on all points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account. The Atmos Summit earns 3 points per dollar spent on eligible dining purchases and all foreign transactions, while the Atmos Ascent earns 2 points per dollar spent at EV charging and gas stations; on local transit (including ride-hailing); and with cable and select streaming services. The Atmos Summit's bonus earnings on foreign transactions are unique in the rewards card space, making the product a fantastic option if you make many purchases outside the U.S. Meanwhile, the Atmos Ascent offers decent earnings across multiple categories, especially for transportation-related expenses and streaming. Winner: Atmos Summit, thanks to higher-value bonus categories (including foreign transactions) — though the Ascent may be better for some everyday spending categories. Redeeming points with the Atmos Ascent vs. the Atmos Summit You can redeem Atmos Rewards points earned on the Atmos Summit or Atmos Ascent in the same ways. Our favorite redemption options are for flights on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld or a partner airline. The program offers outsize value thanks to its popular award chart, which is filled with redemption sweet spots to maximize. I love using Atmos Rewards points to book short-haul American Airlines flights for 4,500 to 6,000 points. However, you can unlock luxurious redemptions with Atmos Rewards too. For instance, you can redeem 75,000 points to fly Japan Airlines business class from the U.S. West Coast to Tokyo. Other Oneworld partners you can book with Atmos Rewards points include British Airways, Fiji Airways and Qantas. Winner: Tie. Both cards share the same redemption options. Transferring points with the Atmos Ascent vs. the Atmos Summit If you have the Atmos Summit, you can transfer your Atmos Rewards points to hotel partners. The Atmos Ascent does not have this feature. These are the hotel loyalty programs you can transfer your Atmos Rewards points to, along with their transfer ratios: - Marriott Bonvoy (1:1) - I Prefer Hotel Rewards (1:2) - Shangri-La Circle (8:1) - Wyndham Rewards (1:1) We generally don't recommend transferring your Atmos Rewards points to hotel partners, since you won't get as high a value as you would using them to book flights. However, if you have a specific redemption in mind and need just a few more points to reach it, it could be a good option. Winner: Atmos Summit. Although we don't recommend using your points this way, you need the Atmos Summit to access this option; you can't transfer Atmos Rewards points with the Atmos Ascent. Should I get the Atmos Ascent or the Atmos Summit? If you're looking for more benefits and higher earning rates, I recommend the Atmos Summit. The card provides solid perks for Alaska and Hawaiian loyalists for a $395 annual fee. However, if you don't need the bonus perks and want a simple card to earn more Atmos Rewards points and receive basic perks when you fly Alaska or Hawaiian, I suggest the Atmos Ascent, since it's a strong option in its own right. Related: Are premium credit cards worth the annual fee? How to upgrade from the Atmos Ascent to the Atmos Summit If you're hoping to upgrade from the Atmos Ascent to the more premium Atmos Summit, you can reach out to Bank of America and request a product change. However, if you opt for an upgrade instead of applying, you may miss out on the Atmos Summit's welcome bonus. So, consider your options before you make a decision. If you hold the Atmos Summit and want to downgrade to the Atmos Ascent, you can also contact Bank of America to make that product change. Related: 4 major considerations before upgrading your credit card Bottom line If you're into premium perks and are loyal to Alaska, Hawaiian or their partners, the Atmos Summit provides fantastic value at a $395 annual fee. However, the Atmos Ascent is a steady option for a lower annual fee. At $95, this card will provide a lot of value for many types of travelers. Ultimately, the right card comes down to how often you fly these airlines and whether you'll fully use the Summit's premium benefits. Frequent flyers will likely justify the higher fee, while more occasional travelers may get better value from the Ascent. To learn more, read our full reviews of the Atmos Ascent and the Atmos Summit. Apply here: Atmos Ascent Apply here: Atmos Summit

item.title: How to easily transfer Avios between all 7 airline loyalty programs
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.90
How to easily transfer Avios between all 7 airline loyalty programs Editor's Note Avios is the rewards currency used by the following airline loyalty programs: - Aer Lingus AerClub - British Airways Club - Finnair Plus - Iberia Club - Loganair Loyalty - Qatar Airways Privilege Club - Vueling Club If you have a loyalty account with any (or all) of these airlines, you can earn and redeem Avios. You can transfer Avios between any of these programs at a ratio of 1:1 in any direction at no cost as often as you like (up to generous annual limits), so 1 British Airways Club Avios is worth 1 Finnair Plus Avios and vice versa. But since each Avios program prices award redemptions slightly differently, you need to have your Avios in the right program to take advantage of sweet spots in each. Fortunately, there is a convenient tool to transfer Avios between all seven programs in one place. How to use the Avios transfer tool To start, ensure you have created a loyalty account with each program you want to transfer Avios to. It's not essential to create accounts for all seven at once; however, it's a good idea to start with at least British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Finnair Plus and Qatar Airways Privilege Club, as these programs generally offer the best value and/or are the most user-friendly. Your accounts must have been open for at least 30 days before you can transfer Avios between accounts. There is no minimum number of Avios to transfer; however, most members are limited to transfers of 999,999 Avios per transaction and 1,000,000 Avios per rolling 12-month period. Ensure you use the same name, email address and date of birth for each account so they can be linked. Then head to the Avios website and log in with any of your affiliated loyalty program account credentials (excluding Qatar Airways Privilege Club; use your British Airways Club details at this point instead). Once you have logged in, select "Transfer now." The Avios balance of the account you logged in with will be shown on the left. Choose any of the other Avios airline loyalty programs you want to link. Note that Avios transfers to and from Qatar Airways Privilege Club must go via British Airways Club, though this process can be done using this tool. How to link your Avios accounts: - Log in to the account you wish to link - Pass the two-factor authentication - Confirm the link (once established, the linked accounts are permanent — so check carefully before submitting) - Your membership number and Avios balance will be shown under each linked account. How to transfer your Avios between programs: Select the programs you want to move your Avios from and to. There is no minimum transfer amount required and no cost for doing so. Complete the two-factor authentication when prompted and wait for the confirmation message. Transfers should be instant. How to earn Avios Aside from having an Avios-earning credit card in your wallet, purchasing Avios or earning rewards with retail partners, most U.S.-based travelers will likely transfer Avios from a credit card program. By earning transferable rewards, you can transfer your points or miles directly to the following Avios-based programs: - American Express Membership Rewards points: Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club and Qatar Airways Privilege Club - Bilt Points: Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club and Qatar Airways Privilege Club - Capital One miles: British Airways Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Finnair Plus - Chase Ultimate Rewards points: Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club and Iberia Club - Citi ThankYou Rewards points: Qatar Airways Privilege Club - Marriott Bonvoy points: Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Vueling Club - Wells Fargo Rewards points: Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club and Iberia Club - Rove miles: Finnair Plus and Qatar Airways Privilege Club These transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, except for Marriott Bonvoy. Marriott points transfer at a 3:1 ratio, with a 5,000 Avios bonus offered for every 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points you transfer (60,000 points become 25,000 Avios, for example). Though not every credit card currency is directly transferable across all seven Avios programs, this tool makes it easy to transfer your rewards between your accounts. For example, if you have Capital One miles and want to book an Iberia award flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD), you can transfer your miles to British Airways Club. Then use the Avios transfer tool to transfer Avios from your British Airways Club account to your Iberia Club account. Related: The Amex transfer bonus I've waited a year for is back: Get 30% more Avios Bottom line While moving Avios between programs might initially seem complicated, it's worth the effort for the excellent flexibility and value it offers.
